A field manual for AI agent harness engineering

Harness Patterns

Every pattern in the classic software design catalog, re-explained through the part of an agent harness where it lives: the loop, the tools, the model layer, memory, subagents and guardrails. Each one comes with an everyday analogy and its own diagram.

192patterns13chapters192diagrams1harness

The harness at a glance

A harness is everything around the model that turns text prediction into a working agent. The chapters follow its parts. Find the box you are building, then read that chapter.

How to read a diagram

Shapes and colours mean the same thing on every page. The orange outline marks the pattern itself, the piece you would write. Orange arrows show the main path; dashed arrows are optional, deferred or reverse flows.

How each entry works

AnalogyAn everyday picture to hold the idea in your head.
Classic definitionWhat the pattern means in general software design.
In the harnessWhere it appears when you build an agent, and why.
Flow and sketchThe steps in order, plus a few lines of Python-style pseudocode.
01
Chapter 1 · Turn control

The Agent Loop

Every agent is a loop: read the context, call the model, act on what it says, repeat until done. These patterns shape that loop: its states, its hooks, how model output is parsed into actions, and how a run can be paused, resumed or rewound.

Game LoopUpdate MethodStateTemplate MethodChain of ResponsibilityInterpreterMementoIteratorCompositeVisitorAcyclic VisitorDouble DispatchCallbackContext ObjectCollecting ParameterPipelineRule EngineTrampoline
1.01

Game Loop

Run the agent as a loop: build context, call the model, execute any tool calls, and repeat until the model stops asking.

Analogy

The ship's navigator taking fixes

Out at sea the navigator does not plot the whole voyage once and walk away. Every hour they read the instruments, mark the position on the chart, set a new heading and wait for the next reading. The ship arrives because the same small cycle repeats, and the voyage ends when the harbour is in sight.

Classic definition

A central loop that repeatedly processes input, updates state and produces output, decoupling the pace of the program from any single event.

In the harness

The heart of every harness is a while loop around the model call. Each iteration sends the system prompt, transcript and tool schemas, then inspects the response: if it contains tool_use blocks, the harness executes them, appends tool_result blocks and goes round again; if stop_reason is end_turn, the loop exits and the final text goes to the user. Guards such as max_turns, a token budget and a cancel flag are checked at the top of every iteration, which is also where compaction and queued user messages are handled.

How it flows
  1. Assemble the request from the system prompt, transcript and tool definitions.
  2. Call the model and stream the response to the UI.
  3. If the response has tool_use blocks, run them and append the tool_result blocks.
  4. Check the stop conditions (end_turn, max_turns, budget, cancel) and loop or exit.
Sketch
while turn < max_turns and not cancelled:
    resp = model.create(system=sys_prompt,
                        messages=msgs,
                        tools=tools)
    msgs.append(resp.as_message())
    calls = [b for b in resp.content
             if b.type == 'tool_use']
    if not calls:
        break  # end_turn: answer is ready
    msgs.append(run_tools(calls))
    turn += 1

Watch outA loop with no turn cap or budget check can spin forever on a model that keeps calling the same failing tool.

1.02

Update Method

Give each harness subsystem its own update hook and let the loop call every one of them once per turn.

Analogy

The zookeeper's feeding round

Every morning the keeper walks the same path past every enclosure. The penguins get fish, the giraffes get acacia, the tortoise gets lettuce and a quick shell check. The keeper does not need to know each animal's diet by heart; each enclosure has its own routine posted on the gate, and the round simply visits them all in turn.

Classic definition

Each object in a simulation implements an update method, and the main loop calls it on every active object once per frame.

In the harness

Between model calls a harness has many small jobs that must advance a little each turn: the token meter recomputes usage, the compactor checks whether the context window is near its threshold, a todo tracker nudges the model if the list is stale, and a poller collects finished background tasks. Rather than hard-coding all of this into the loop body, each subsystem registers an object with an on_turn(ctx) method. The loop iterates the registered list once per turn, so adding a new behaviour is one registration, not an edit to the loop.

How it flows
  1. Subsystems register objects that implement on_turn(ctx).
  2. At the top of each turn the loop builds a TurnContext.
  3. The loop calls on_turn(ctx) on every registered object in order.
  4. Each object reads or adjusts the context, then the model call proceeds.
Sketch
class Compactor:
    def on_turn(self, ctx):
        if ctx.tokens > 0.8 * ctx.window:
            ctx.msgs = summarise(ctx.msgs)

systems = [BudgetMeter(), Compactor(),
           TaskPoller(), TodoNudger()]

for turn in agent_loop():
    for s in systems:
        s.on_turn(turn.ctx)

Watch outUpdates that depend on each other's results make the registration order load-bearing, so document it or merge those systems.

1.03

State

Model the loop's lifecycle as explicit state objects so each state decides how to react to input, interrupts and tool results.

Analogy

The laundromat washing machine

Press the start button on a washing machine and what happens depends on where it is in the cycle. While filling, the door can still open; during the spin it stays locked and the button does nothing; once finished, the light turns green and the door releases. The same button, a different response, because each stage has its own rules.

Classic definition

Let an object change its behaviour when its internal state changes, by delegating to a separate object for each state.

In the harness

An agent session moves through clear phases: Idle, CallingModel, AwaitingApproval, RunningTool and Done. The same event means different things in each: a new user message starts a turn when Idle, is queued while RunningTool, and an Esc keypress cancels the stream in CallingModel but counts as a denial in AwaitingApproval. Implementing each phase as a state class with on_message, on_interrupt and on_tool_result methods replaces a tangle of if-statements, and makes illegal transitions (running a tool without approval) impossible to write by accident.

How it flows
  1. The session holds a reference to its current state object.
  2. Every event (message, interrupt, model response, approval) is forwarded to that state.
  3. The state handles the event and returns the next state.
  4. The session swaps in the new state and the UI reflects it.
Sketch
class AwaitingApproval(State):
    def on_approve(self, s):
        return RunningTool(self.call)
    def on_deny(self, s):
        s.add_result(self.call, 'denied')
        return CallingModel()
    def on_message(self, s, m):
        s.queue.append(m)  # hold it
        return self

Watch outDo not let tools or hooks set the state field directly; every transition should go through the current state's methods.

1.04

Template Method

Fix the order of a turn in a base class and let each agent type override only the hooks it needs.

Analogy

The builder's standard house plan

A housing developer builds every home in the same order: foundation, frame, roof, then interiors. Buyers choose the kitchen tiles, the bathroom fittings and the paint, but nobody gets to put the roof on before the walls. The plan is fixed; the choices are slots within it.

Classic definition

Define the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class method and let subclasses override specific steps without changing its structure.

In the harness

A harness base class defines run_turn(): build the system prompt, trim context, call the model, dispatch tool calls, record the turn. That method is final. A coding agent overrides system_prompt() to add repository rules and on_tool_result() to run a linter after edits; a research subagent overrides only select_tools() to restrict itself to search and fetch. Because the skeleton never changes, invariants such as logging every turn to the transcript and checking the token budget before each call hold for every agent type.

How it flows
  1. The base class implements run_turn() as a fixed sequence of steps.
  2. Some steps call hook methods that have default implementations.
  3. A subclass overrides the hooks it cares about and nothing else.
  4. Every agent type runs the same skeleton with its own variations.
Sketch
class BaseAgent:
    def run_turn(self, msgs):  # fixed
        sp = self.system_prompt()  # hook
        resp = self.model.create(
            system=sp, messages=msgs)
        for call in resp.tool_calls:
            out = self.tools.run(call)
            self.on_tool_result(call, out)
        self.transcript.record(resp)
class CodingAgent(BaseAgent):
    def system_prompt(self):
        return BASE + REPO_RULES

Watch outIf subclasses start overriding run_turn() itself, the guarantees vanish; mark it final and add a new hook instead.

1.05

Chain of Responsibility

Pass each tool call through an ordered chain of hooks; any hook can allow, modify or block it, or pass it on.

Analogy

Airport departure checkpoints

Between the kerb and the aircraft door a passenger meets the check-in desk, passport control, the security scanner and the gate agent. Each one checks a single thing and either waves you through to the next or stops you there. None of them needs to know what the others check, and the airport can add a new checkpoint without retraining the rest.

Classic definition

Give more than one object a chance to handle a request by linking the handlers in a chain and passing the request along until one handles it.

In the harness

Before a tool call executes, the harness runs it through a chain of PreToolUse hooks: an allowlist check, a path guard that rejects writes outside the workspace, a secrets scanner, and finally an interactive approval prompt. Each hook receives the call and returns allow, deny, modify or pass. A deny short-circuits the chain and becomes an error tool_result the model can read; pass hands the call to the next hook. Users and plugins append their own hooks through settings without touching harness code.

How it flows
  1. The model emits a tool_use block and the harness wraps it as a request.
  2. The first hook inspects it and returns allow, deny, modify or pass.
  3. On pass the request moves to the next hook; on deny the chain stops.
  4. If it reaches the end, the tool runs with the possibly modified input.
Sketch
class PathGuard(Hook):
    def handle(self, call, nxt):
        p = call.input.get('path', '')
        if p and not p.startswith(WORKSPACE):
            return Deny('outside workspace')
        return nxt(call)

chain = [Allowlist(), PathGuard(),
         SecretScan(), AskUser()]
result = run_chain(chain, call, execute)

Watch outLong chains hide which hook made the decision; log the deciding hook's name with every allow and deny.

1.06

Interpreter

Parse the model's structured output into a small grammar of action objects, then evaluate that tree against the workspace.

Analogy

The knitting pattern

A knitting pattern reads like code: "k2, p2, repeat to end; row 3: k all". The knitter does not improvise; they read each abbreviation, turn it into a stitch, and apply repeats and row instructions as rules. A tiny language with a few words produces a whole jumper.

Classic definition

Define a grammar for a simple language, represent sentences as a tree of expression objects, and evaluate the tree by calling interpret on each node.

In the harness

Some harnesses let the model answer in a compact action language instead of one tool call per step, for example an edit block format or a plan DSL with steps like edit, run and if_fail. The harness parses that text into a tree of expression nodes (Seq, Edit, Run, OnFail), and each node's interpret(ctx) method performs its part against the workspace. Parse errors are returned to the model as a tool_result so it can correct its syntax on the next turn.

How it flows
  1. The model returns text in the agreed action syntax.
  2. A parser turns the text into a tree of expression objects.
  3. The harness calls interpret(ctx) on the root node.
  4. Each node acts on the workspace and passes results to its children or parent.
Sketch
class Seq(Expr):
    def interpret(self, ctx):
        return [s.interpret(ctx)
                for s in self.steps]

class Edit(Expr):
    def interpret(self, ctx):
        return ctx.fs.patch(self.path,
                            self.diff)

tree = parse(model_text)  # Seq([Edit, Run])
results = tree.interpret(ctx)

Watch outKeep the grammar tiny; once it needs variables and loops you are building a programming language, and a sandboxed real one is safer.

1.07

Memento

Snapshot the session's messages and file edits before each risky step so the user can rewind to any earlier turn.

Analogy

The film set continuity photo

Before the crew breaks for lunch, the continuity supervisor photographs the set: the half-full glass, the open book, the actor's loosened tie. She does not need to understand why each prop is where it is. After lunch, the photo lets everyone put the scene back exactly as it was so the next take matches.

Classic definition

Capture an object's internal state in an opaque snapshot, without breaking encapsulation, so the object can be restored to that state later.

In the harness

Before each turn that edits files, the session creates a checkpoint: a copy of the message list plus the original contents of every file the turn is about to change. A checkpoint store keeps these snapshots by turn number without inspecting them. When the user runs a rewind command, the session restores the chosen checkpoint, rewriting the files and truncating the transcript, so both the conversation and the workspace return to that point. Long sessions keep only recent checkpoints or store file diffs to limit disk use.

How it flows
  1. Before a turn with edits, the session builds a snapshot of messages and touched files.
  2. The checkpoint store saves it under the turn number.
  3. The user asks to rewind to an earlier turn.
  4. The store hands back that snapshot and the session restores itself from it.
Sketch
class Session:
    def checkpoint(self):
        files = self.fs.copy(self.touched)
        return Snapshot(self.msgs[:], files)
    def restore(self, snap):
        self.msgs = list(snap.msgs)
        self.fs.write_all(snap.files)

store[turn] = session.checkpoint()
session.restore(store[6])  # /rewind 6

Watch outSnapshots cannot undo side effects outside the workspace, such as a sent message or a deployed build, so say so when the user rewinds.

1.08

Iterator

Walk stream events, turns or stored messages one at a time through next(), without loading or exposing the whole source.

Analogy

The sushi conveyor belt

At a conveyor sushi bar you never see the kitchen's order list. Plates arrive in front of you one at a time and you take the next one when you are ready. Whether the chef is slicing fresh fish or pulling from the fridge, your side of the counter works the same way.

Classic definition

Provide a way to access the elements of a collection sequentially without exposing its underlying representation.

In the harness

A streaming model response arrives as server-sent events: message_start, content_block_delta, content_block_stop and so on. The SDK wraps the raw byte stream in an async iterator so the harness can write async for event in stream and render text deltas as they arrive. The same idea applies elsewhere: a transcript iterator that reads JSONL lines lazily from disk, and a paginated iterator over a long history that fetches the next page only when the consumer asks. Consumers never care whether the items come from a socket, a file or an API.

How it flows
  1. The source (stream, file, paged API) is wrapped in an iterator object.
  2. The consumer asks for the next item.
  3. The iterator reads just enough of the source to produce one item.
  4. When the source is exhausted the iterator signals the end and the loop stops.
Sketch
async for ev in client.stream(req):
    if ev.type == 'content_block_delta':
        ui.append(ev.delta.text)
    elif ev.type == 'message_stop':
        break

def turns(path):  # lazy over a JSONL file
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            yield json.loads(line)

Watch outAn iterator over a live stream can be consumed only once; buffer the events if both the UI and the transcript writer need them.

1.09

Composite

Treat a message, a tool result and a single text block through the same interface, because content blocks nest inside each other.

Analogy

Freight on a warehouse pallet

A pallet holds cartons, a carton holds boxes, and a box holds individual items. The forklift scale weighs any of them the same way: put it on, read the number. A carton's weight is just the sum of what is inside, so nobody needs a special procedure for each level.

Classic definition

Compose objects into tree structures and let clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly.

In the harness

A message's content is a list of blocks: text, image, tool_use and tool_result, and a tool_result can itself contain text and image blocks. The harness gives every block the same small interface, such as token_count(), render() and redact(). Leaves answer directly; containers like Message and ToolResult delegate to their children and combine the answers. Counting the tokens of a whole transcript becomes one call on the root instead of a nested set of loops with type checks.

How it flows
  1. Define one Block interface with the operations the harness needs.
  2. Implement leaves (TextBlock, ImageBlock) to answer directly.
  3. Implement containers (Message, ToolResult) to loop over their children.
  4. Callers invoke the operation on any node, from a single block to a full transcript.
Sketch
class TextBlock(Block):
    def tokens(self):
        return count(self.text)

class ToolResult(Block):
    def tokens(self):
        return 8 + sum(c.tokens()
                       for c in self.content)

total = sum(m.tokens() for m in transcript)

Watch outDo not force operations that make no sense for every block onto the shared interface; a leaf with fifteen no-op methods is a smell.

1.10

Visitor

Keep content block classes stable and put each cross-cutting operation, such as token counting or redaction, in its own visitor class.

Analogy

The fire safety inspector at the mall

A fire inspector walks through a shopping centre: the bakery, the cinema, the pharmacy. Each shop lets the inspector in and shows what matters for its kind of business, the ovens, the projection booth, the chemical store. Next month a different inspector, for accessibility, walks the same route with a different checklist, and the shops change nothing.

Classic definition

Represent an operation to be performed on the elements of an object structure as a separate object, letting you add operations without changing the element classes.

In the harness

Content blocks rarely change, but the operations run over them keep growing: count tokens, redact secrets before logging, render to terminal, render to HTML, convert to another provider's format. With Visitor, each block has a single accept(v) method that calls v.visit_text(self), v.visit_tool_use(self) and so on. A new operation is a new visitor class with one method per block type, and the block classes and the transcript walker stay untouched.

How it flows
  1. Each block class implements accept(visitor) by calling the matching visit method.
  2. An operation is written as a visitor class with one visit method per block type.
  3. The harness walks the transcript and calls block.accept(visitor) on each block.
  4. The visitor accumulates its result, such as a token total or a redacted copy.
Sketch
class ToolUseBlock(Block):
    def accept(self, v):
        return v.visit_tool_use(self)

class Redactor(Visitor):
    def visit_text(self, b):
        return scrub(b.text)
    def visit_tool_use(self, b):
        return {**b.input, 'api_key': '***'}

clean = [b.accept(Redactor()) for b in blocks]

Watch outAdding a new block type means updating every visitor; if new block types arrive often, prefer Acyclic Visitor or plain methods on the blocks.

1.11

Acyclic Visitor

Let each visitor handle only the block types it knows, so a new content block type never forces edits elsewhere.

Analogy

The museum's specialist tours

A museum runs a sculpture tour, a paintings tour and a textiles tour. Each guide stops only at the exhibits they know and walks straight past the rest. When the museum opens a new photography wing, it hires a photography guide; nobody retrains the sculpture guide.

Classic definition

A Visitor variant that drops the single interface listing every element type; each visitor implements small per-type interfaces and elements check for them at runtime.

In the harness

Content block types keep arriving: thinking blocks, citations, documents, server tool results. In a classic Visitor every new type means a new method on every visitor. In the acyclic version, ImageBlock.accept(v) checks whether v implements ImageVisitor and calls visit_image only if it does. A thumbnail generator implements ImageVisitor alone, a secret redactor implements TextVisitor and ToolUseVisitor, and a new DocumentBlock ships with its own DocumentVisitor interface without touching either.

How it flows
  1. Declare one small visitor interface per block type.
  2. Each visitor class implements only the interfaces it needs.
  3. A block's accept(v) checks whether v supports its type.
  4. If it does, the block calls the visit method; otherwise it skips or uses a default.
Sketch
class ImageVisitor(Protocol):
    def visit_image(self, b): ...

class ImageBlock(Block):
    def accept(self, v):
        if isinstance(v, ImageVisitor):
            return v.visit_image(self)
        return None  # visitor ignores images

class Thumbnailer(ImageVisitor):
    def visit_image(self, b):
        return shrink(b.data, 256)

Watch outThe runtime type check moves errors from compile time to run time, so test that each visitor really handles the types it claims.

1.12

Double Dispatch

Choose the handler from two runtime types at once, the incoming event type and the session's current state.

Analogy

The referee's foul call

A football referee's decision depends on two things together: what the foul was and where it happened. A trip in midfield is a free kick; the same trip inside the box is a penalty; a handball on the goal line may add a red card. The rulebook is a grid of foul type against pitch position, not one list.

Classic definition

A technique that selects the method to call based on the runtime types of two objects, typically by having the first object call back into the second.

In the harness

The harness receives several event types (UserMessage, Interrupt, ToolResult, ApprovalReply) while the session can be in several states (Idle, Streaming, RunningTool). The right action depends on both: a UserMessage in Idle starts a turn, in RunningTool it is queued; an Interrupt in Streaming aborts the request, in RunningTool it kills the child process. The event's dispatch(state) method calls state.on_user_message(self) or state.on_interrupt(self), so the language's method lookup picks the cell in the event x state grid with no type switches.

How it flows
  1. An event arrives and the harness calls event.dispatch(current_state).
  2. The event calls back the state method named for its own type.
  3. That state method runs the behaviour for this event in this state.
  4. It returns the next state, which handles the following event.
Sketch
class Interrupt(Event):
    def dispatch(self, state):
        return state.on_interrupt(self)

class RunningTool(State):
    def on_interrupt(self, ev):
        self.proc.kill()
        return Idle()
    def on_user_message(self, ev):
        self.pending.append(ev)
        return self

Watch outThe grid grows as types times states; when most cells share a default, a small lookup table is easier to read than many methods.

1.13

Callback

Pass functions into the loop that it calls when a token streams in, a tool finishes or a turn completes.

Analogy

The garage that rings you

You drop your car at the garage and leave a note: call this number when it is ready, and text me if a repair will cost more than two hundred pounds. You go about your day. The mechanic does not need to know who you are or what you will do next; they just ring the number at the right moments.

Classic definition

Pass executable code as an argument to other code, which calls it back at a suitable time.

In the harness

An agent loop is shared by a terminal UI, a web client, an SDK script and an eval runner, and each wants to react to different moments. The loop accepts callbacks such as on_text_delta, on_tool_start, on_tool_end and on_turn_complete, and invokes them at those points. The terminal prints deltas, the web client pushes them over a websocket, and the eval runner ignores deltas but records every tool call. The loop itself never imports any UI code.

How it flows
  1. The caller passes callback functions when it starts a run.
  2. The loop stores them and starts calling the model.
  3. At each event (text delta, tool start, tool end) it calls the matching callback.
  4. When the turn completes it calls on_done with the final message.
Sketch
def show(delta):
    term.write(delta.text)

def save(msg):
    transcript.append(msg)

agent.run(prompt,
          on_text_delta=show,
          on_tool_end=lambda c, r: log(c, r),
          on_done=save)

Watch outA slow or failing callback blocks or crashes the loop; time-box callbacks and catch their exceptions so the turn still completes.

1.14

Context Object

Bundle everything one turn needs (ids, budget, working directory, permissions, cancel token) into one object passed to every component.

Analogy

The patient's travelling folder

When a hospital patient moves from admissions to X-ray to surgery, a folder travels on the trolley with them. It holds the wristband number, allergies, consent forms and the doctor's notes. Every department reads what it needs from the same folder instead of phoning the others.

Classic definition

Encapsulate state and services needed across several layers in a single object that is passed along, instead of threading many separate parameters.

In the harness

Every turn touches many components: the model client, the tool runner, hooks, the tracer and subagent spawners. Each needs some of the session id, turn number, working directory, permission mode, token budget remaining, abort signal and trace span. The harness builds a TurnContext at the start of the turn and passes that single object down every call. Adding a field, such as the active MCP servers, changes the context class and its readers, not every function signature in between.

How it flows
  1. At the start of a turn the loop builds a TurnContext.
  2. It passes ctx to the model client, tool runner and hooks.
  3. Each component reads the fields it needs and may record usage back.
  4. When the turn ends the context is discarded or archived with the trace.
Sketch
@dataclass
class TurnContext:
    session_id: str
    turn: int
    cwd: Path
    perms: PermissionMode
    budget: TokenBudget
    cancel: AbortSignal

ctx = TurnContext(sid, n, cwd, mode, b, sig)
resp = model.call(msgs, ctx)
out = tools.run(resp.tool_calls, ctx)

Watch outA context object that collects every global in the system becomes a hidden dependency bag; keep it per turn and keep it small.

1.15

Collecting Parameter

Pass one accumulator object through a sequence of steps so each step adds its findings instead of returning separate results to merge.

Analogy

The wedding guest book

At a wedding the guest book travels from table to table. Each guest writes a line and passes it on. At the end of the night the couple has one book with every message, and nobody had to gather loose cards from each table.

Classic definition

Pass a collecting object into methods so each can add its results to it, building up a combined result across many calls.

In the harness

A code review subagent runs several checks: grep for TODOs, scan the diff for secrets, run the tests, check the changelog. Each check receives the same Findings object and appends issues with file, line and severity. After the last check, the subagent turns the collected findings into a single report message for the orchestrator. The same shape appears when a harness gathers usage across sub-calls: one UsageCollector is passed into every model call and tool call, and the turn total is read from it at the end.

How it flows
  1. Create an empty collector at the start of the task.
  2. Pass it into each step or tool wrapper.
  3. Each step appends what it found or what it used.
  4. Read the collector once at the end to build the report or totals.
Sketch
findings = Findings()
check_todos(diff, findings)
scan_secrets(diff, findings)
run_tests(repo, findings)

def scan_secrets(diff, out):
    for ln in diff.added_lines():
        if KEY_RE.search(ln.text):
            out.add(ln.path, ln.no, 'high')
report = findings.to_markdown()

Watch outIf steps run in parallel, the collector needs a lock or each step should return its own list to merge afterwards.

1.16

Pipeline

Prepare context in fixed stages: retrieve candidates, rerank them, compress the winners, then inject them into the prompt.

Analogy

The water treatment works

River water passes through screens that catch branches, settling tanks where silt sinks, sand filters, and finally a disinfection stage. Each stage does one job and hands cleaner water to the next. Engineers can upgrade the filters without touching the screens.

Classic definition

Process data through a series of stages where each stage's output is the next stage's input, so stages can be built, tested and replaced independently.

In the harness

Before calling the model, a retrieval-augmented harness runs a context pipeline. The retriever pulls fifty chunks from a vector store and keyword index, a reranker scores them against the query and keeps eight, a compressor trims each to the relevant sentences, and an injector formats them as document blocks in the prompt with source ids. Each stage has the signature list in, list out, so a team can swap the reranker model or add a deduplication stage without touching the others, and evals can score each stage separately.

How it flows
  1. The user's query enters the first stage.
  2. Retrieve returns a broad set of candidate chunks.
  3. Rerank and compress narrow and shorten the set.
  4. Inject formats the survivors into the context window for the model call.
Sketch
stages = [retrieve(k=50), rerank(top=8),
          compress(max_tokens=2000), inject]

def run(query):
    data = query
    for stage in stages:
        data = stage(data)
    return data  # prompt-ready blocks

prompt = run(user_msg)

Watch outEach stage can drop the one chunk that mattered; log what each stage removed so a bad answer can be traced to its stage.

1.17

Rule Engine

Evaluate a set of declarative rules against each turn's facts to decide routing, approvals and compaction without hard-coded branches.

Analogy

The insurance claims desk

A claims handler works from a rulebook, not from instinct. Claims under five hundred pounds with photos are paid at once; anything mentioning flood goes to a specialist; a third claim in a year triggers a fraud check. When the company changes its policy, it edits the rulebook and the handlers apply the new rules the next morning.

Classic definition

Separate business rules from application code by expressing them as condition-action pairs that an engine evaluates against a set of facts.

In the harness

Each turn the harness gathers facts: context usage, the requested tool and its arguments, the user's plan tier, the working directory, the time of day. A rule engine evaluates rules loaded from a settings file, such as: if the context is over 80 percent, compact first; if the command matches rm -rf, require approval; if the task is classified as simple, route to a smaller model. Matching rules produce actions that the loop applies in priority order. Operators change behaviour by editing rules, and the rules can be tested against recorded turns.

How it flows
  1. Load the rules from configuration at startup or on change.
  2. At each turn, collect the facts into a dictionary.
  3. Evaluate every rule's condition against the facts.
  4. Apply the actions of matching rules in priority order.
Sketch
RULES = [
  Rule(lambda f: f['ctx_pct'] > 80,
       'compact_first', prio=1),
  Rule(lambda f: 'rm -rf' in f['cmd'],
       'require_approval', prio=0),
  Rule(lambda f: f['task'] == 'simple',
       'use_small_model', prio=2)]

hits = [r for r in RULES if r.when(facts)]
for r in sorted(hits, key=lambda r: r.prio):
    apply(r.action)

Watch outRules that interact (one rule's action changing another's facts) become hard to reason about; keep actions independent or evaluate once per turn.

1.18

Trampoline

Run deep recursive planning as a flat loop where each step returns the next step instead of calling it.

Analogy

The choose-your-own-adventure book

Reading a choose-your-own-adventure book, you could keep a finger in every page you passed through, but you would soon run out of fingers. Instead you read the instruction at the bottom, "turn to page 84", and flip there. You only ever hold one place in the book, however long the story runs.

Classic definition

Execute recursive functions in a loop by having each call return a thunk describing the next call, which a driver loop invokes until a final value appears.

In the harness

An agent that decomposes a goal into subgoals, and subgoals into smaller ones, is naturally recursive. Written as nested function calls, a long plan can hit Python's recursion limit and holds every intermediate frame in memory. With a trampoline, plan_step returns either Bounce(fn, args) for the next subgoal or Done(result). A small driver loop keeps calling bounces, which also gives the harness a natural place to check the turn budget, save a checkpoint and honour a cancel request between steps.

How it flows
  1. Rewrite the recursive planner so it returns the next call instead of making it.
  2. The driver loop calls the first step.
  3. While the result is a Bounce, the driver calls the function it carries.
  4. When a Done arrives, the driver returns its value.
Sketch
def plan(goal, acc):
    sub = model.next_subgoal(goal, acc)
    if sub is None:
        return Done(acc)
    return Bounce(plan, goal, acc + [sub])

def trampoline(r):
    while isinstance(r, Bounce):
        budget.check(); cancel.check()
        r = r.fn(*r.args)
    return r.value

Watch outTrampolining adds indirection to code that rarely goes deep; use it only when recursion depth depends on model output you do not control.

02
Chapter 2 · The agent's hands

The Tool System

Tools are how a model touches the world. This chapter covers how tool calls are represented, discovered, created, wrapped, guarded and executed, and why almost every Gang of Four pattern finds a home here.

CommandStrategyAdapterConverterFacadeRegistryFactoryFactory MethodAbstract FactoryFactory KitBuilderStep BuilderPrototypeProxyVirtual ProxyDynamic ProxyDecoratorDelegationServantNull ObjectSpecial CaseExtension ObjectsMarker InterfaceType ObjectBytecodeAbstract DocumentPropertyParameter ObjectExecute AroundFluent Interface
2.01

Command

Turn every tool call into an object that can be queued, logged, approved, retried or undone.

Analogy

The restaurant order ticket

A waiter does not cook. They write your order on a ticket and clip it to the rail. The ticket can wait in line, be read by any free cook, be checked by the head chef, and be torn up if you change your mind. The ticket is the order, separated from whoever fulfils it.

Classic definition

Encapsulate a request as an object, so callers can parameterise, queue, log and undo operations without knowing how they run.

In the harness

When the model emits a tool_use block, the harness wraps it in a ToolCommand holding the tool name, arguments and call id. That object travels through the permission gate, the execution queue and the transcript. Because the call is data rather than an immediate function call, the harness can pause it for user approval, replay it in an eval, log it for audit, or run a compensating undo when a later step fails.

How it flows
  1. The model returns a tool_use block with name, input and id.
  2. The harness builds a ToolCommand and places it on the execution queue.
  3. A permission check approves, edits or rejects the command.
  4. The executor runs it, records the result, and keeps undo data when the tool supports it.
Sketch
class ToolCommand:
    def __init__(self, tool, args, cid):
        self.tool, self.args = tool, args
        self.id = cid
    def execute(self):
        return self.tool.run(**self.args)
    def undo(self):
        return self.tool.revert(self.id)

cmd = ToolCommand(tools['write_file'],
                  block.input, block.id)
queue.put(cmd)

Watch outCommands that touch the outside world (sent email, paid invoice) often cannot be undone, so mark them irreversible and require approval up front.

2.02

Strategy

Keep one tool name and schema while swapping the implementation behind it, such as which backend a search tool queries.

Analogy

Interchangeable camera lenses

A photographer keeps the same camera body all day and twists on a different lens for a portrait, a landscape or a distant bird. The shutter button, the viewfinder and the memory card never change. Only the glass in front decides how the light is gathered.

Classic definition

Define a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface so the caller can pick one at runtime without changing its own code.

In the harness

The model sees a single web_search tool with a fixed input schema: query and max_results. Behind it the harness holds a SearchStrategy interface with several implementations: a hosted search API, a vector store over the user's documents, or a local ripgrep when the machine is offline. Configuration or the workspace type picks the strategy at session start, so the tool definition in the system prompt stays byte-identical and the prompt cache keeps hitting. Evals inject a canned strategy that returns fixed results.

How it flows
  1. The harness reads its config and picks a SearchStrategy for this session.
  2. The web_search tool is registered with one schema whatever the choice.
  3. The model emits a tool_use block for web_search with a query.
  4. The tool delegates to the chosen strategy and formats its hits as one tool_result.
Sketch
class SearchStrategy(Protocol):
    def search(self, q, k): ...

class WebSearchTool:
    name = 'web_search'
    def __init__(self, strategy):
        self.strategy = strategy
    def run(self, query, max_results=5):
        hits = self.strategy.search(
            query, max_results)
        return format_hits(hits)

tool = WebSearchTool(STRATEGIES[cfg.search])

Watch outIf strategies return results of different shape or quality, the model cannot learn what the tool does; normalise every strategy's output to one format.

2.03

Adapter

Wrap MCP servers and external APIs so each one looks like a native tool with the harness's own name, schema and run method.

Analogy

The travel plug adapter

You land in London with a laptop charger built for American sockets. You do not rewire the charger or rip out the wall socket. A small plastic block takes two flat pins on one side and offers three square pins on the other. The charger and the socket each keep their own shape, and only the adapter knows both.

Classic definition

Convert the interface of an existing class into the interface a client expects, so classes with incompatible interfaces can work together.

In the harness

The agent loop knows one contract: a Tool with a name, a description, an input_schema and run(args) returning a ToolResult. An MCP server speaks JSON-RPC instead, with tools/list and tools/call, and a REST API speaks HTTP with its own auth headers and status codes. The harness writes one adapter per foreign source: an MCP adapter maps tools/call replies into ToolResult and turns isError into an error result, and an HTTP adapter maps 4xx and 5xx responses the same way. The loop, the permission gate and the transcript never learn where a tool really lives.

How it flows
  1. At startup the harness connects to each MCP server and lists its tools.
  2. It wraps every remote tool in an adapter that implements the Tool interface.
  3. The model calls the tool by name, exactly like a built-in.
  4. The adapter turns the call into tools/call or HTTP and maps the reply back into a ToolResult.
Sketch
class McpToolAdapter(Tool):
    def __init__(self, client, spec):
        self.client, self.spec = client, spec
        self.name = 'mcp__' + spec.name
    def run(self, args):
        r = self.client.call_tool(
            self.spec.name, args)
        return ToolResult(
            content=r.content,
            is_error=r.isError)

Watch outAn adapter that turns remote failures into empty successes misleads the model; carry errors and timeouts through as is_error results.

2.04

Converter

Translate tool specs, calls and results between the harness's internal types and each provider's wire format, in both directions.

Analogy

The interpreter at a summit

In a glass booth at the back of the hall, an interpreter hears a minister speak French and says the same words in English into the delegates' headsets, then does the reverse when the reply comes. Neither minister learns the other's language. The meaning stays the same; only the form changes, and it changes in both directions.

Classic definition

A dedicated object that converts between two representations of the same data, usually with a matching function for each direction.

In the harness

Inside the harness a tool is a ToolSpec, a call is a ToolCall and an output is a ToolResult. Each model provider wants something else on the wire: one expects input_schema at the top level, another nests parameters under a function key, and results go back as tool_result content blocks with text, image or error parts. A provider converter owns all of these mappings: spec to wire, tool_use block to ToolCall, ToolResult to content blocks. Adding a provider then touches one class, and round-trip tests can prove that nothing is lost.

How it flows
  1. Before a request, the converter turns each ToolSpec into the provider's tool format.
  2. When the response arrives, it parses each tool_use block into a ToolCall.
  3. After execution, it turns each ToolResult into a tool_result content block.
  4. Round-trip tests check that converting out and back yields an equal object.
Sketch
class MessagesConverter:
    def spec_out(self, s):
        return {'name': s.name,
                'description': s.desc,
                'input_schema': s.schema}
    def call_in(self, block):
        return ToolCall(block.id, block.name,
                        block.input)
    def result_out(self, r):
        return {'type': 'tool_result',
                'tool_use_id': r.call_id,
                'content': r.blocks,
                'is_error': r.is_error}

Watch outConverters drift silently when a provider adds a new block type; fail loudly on unknown types instead of dropping them.

2.05

Facade

Expose one simple tool to the model that hides a multi-step subsystem, so the model makes one call instead of five.

Analogy

The hotel concierge desk

A guest says: dinner for four at eight, and a taxi there. The concierge phones the restaurant, books the car, checks the traffic and hands back one card with the time and the table. The guest never sees the phone list, the taxi firm's dispatch system or the reservation book.

Classic definition

Provide a single simplified interface to a complex subsystem, reducing what clients must know about its parts.

In the harness

Running a project's tests in a fresh sandbox means booting a container, installing dependencies, invoking the test runner, parsing a JUnit XML report and trimming megabytes of logs. Exposed as five tools, the model would spend turns and context orchestrating them and could run them in the wrong order. A run_tests facade takes one optional path filter, performs every step internally and returns a short summary of failures. The subsystem pieces stay available to harness code and to other facades, but the model's tool list stays small.

How it flows
  1. The model calls run_tests with an optional path filter.
  2. The facade boots or reuses the sandbox and installs dependencies.
  3. It runs the test runner and parses the report.
  4. It returns a short summary of failing tests as one tool_result.
Sketch
def run_tests(path='.'):
    box = sandbox.acquire(repo)
    deps.install(box, lockfile='uv.lock')
    raw = runner.run(box, 'pytest', path)
    rep = junit.parse(raw.xml)
    return summarise(rep.failures,
                     max_tokens=800)

Watch outA facade that hides too much leaves the model stuck when something unusual breaks; include a log path so it can dig deeper.

2.06

Registry

Keep one name-to-tool map that the harness uses both to list tools for the model and to dispatch each tool_use call.

Analogy

The coat check at a concert hall

Every coat handed over gets a numbered tag and a matching hook. At the interval nobody searches the racks; you show tag 214 and the attendant walks straight to hook 214. Coats from the matinee and the evening show share one system, and a missing number is noticed at once.

Classic definition

A well-known object that other objects use to find shared objects and services by name.

In the harness

Built-in tools, tools adapted from MCP servers and plugin tools all register into one ToolRegistry at startup, keyed by a unique name such as read_file or mcp__github__create_issue. The registry produces the tools array sent with each request, and when a tool_use block arrives the dispatcher looks up block.name and calls that handler. Duplicate names fail at registration instead of at call time, and an unknown name returns an is_error tool_result so the model can correct itself.

How it flows
  1. Each tool source registers its tools by unique name at startup.
  2. The registry lists schemas for the request's tools array.
  3. A tool_use block arrives and the dispatcher calls registry.get(block.name).
  4. The handler runs, or an unknown name returns an error result.
Sketch
class ToolRegistry:
    def __init__(self):
        self._tools = {}
    def register(self, tool):
        if tool.name in self._tools:
            raise DuplicateTool(tool.name)
        self._tools[tool.name] = tool
    def get(self, name):
        return self._tools.get(name)
    def schemas(self):
        return [t.spec() for t in
                self._tools.values()]

Watch outChanging the registry mid-session changes the tools array and breaks the prompt cache; freeze it per session or only append.

2.07

Factory

Create tool instances from a name and a config entry, so agent definitions list tools as data instead of constructing them in code.

Analogy

The car rental desk

You tell the clerk: compact, automatic, three days, and you get a key fob. You never walk the lot, check the oil or register the plate. Behind the desk someone picks a car of the right class, fuels it and fills in the paperwork, and the same desk hands out vans and convertibles too.

Classic definition

An object whose job is to create other objects, hiding which concrete class is instantiated behind a single creation call.

In the harness

An agent definition file says tools: [bash, web_fetch, read_file], with per-tool settings such as a timeout or an allowed domain list. A ToolFactory maps each name to a constructor, injects shared dependencies like the sandbox handle, the HTTP client and credentials, and returns ready Tool objects. Subagent definitions, eval configs and user settings all go through the same factory, so a tool is always built the same way with the same safety defaults.

How it flows
  1. The harness loads the agent definition and its tools list.
  2. For each entry it calls ToolFactory.create(name, settings).
  3. The factory picks the class, injects shared dependencies and applies defaults.
  4. The finished tools are registered for the session.
Sketch
class ToolFactory:
    def __init__(self, deps):
        self.deps = deps
    def create(self, name, cfg):
        if name == 'bash':
            return BashTool(
                self.deps.box, cfg.timeout)
        if name == 'web_fetch':
            return WebFetch(
                self.deps.http, cfg.domains)
        raise UnknownTool(name)

Watch outWhen creation is one constructor call with no shared dependencies, a factory only adds indirection; call the class directly.

2.08

Factory Method

Let a base runner own the agent workflow while each subclass decides which concrete executor or tool it creates.

Analogy

A shipping firm's two divisions

Head office writes one delivery procedure: collect the parcel, load the vehicle, track it, get a signature. The road division fills the load step with a lorry and the sea division with a container ship. The procedure never changes; each division only decides which vehicle it brings.

Classic definition

Define a method for creating an object in a base class, but let subclasses decide which class to instantiate.

In the harness

A BaseRunner implements the turn loop, the approval flow and transcript writing, and calls self.make_shell() whenever it needs a command executor. LocalRunner overrides make_shell to return a shell on the user's machine; CloudRunner returns one inside a container with no network access. Tests subclass once more and return a fake shell that replays recorded output. The loop is written and tested once, and only the creation step varies.

How it flows
  1. BaseRunner.run() starts the loop and needs an executor.
  2. It calls its own make_shell() method instead of a constructor.
  3. The subclass override returns a local shell, a sandbox shell or a fake.
  4. The loop uses the returned shell through the common interface.
Sketch
class BaseRunner:
    def run(self, task):
        shell = self.make_shell()
        return self.loop(task, shell)
    def make_shell(self):
        raise NotImplementedError

class LocalRunner(BaseRunner):
    def make_shell(self):
        return LocalShell(cwd=self.repo)

class CloudRunner(BaseRunner):
    def make_shell(self):
        return SandboxShell(net=False)

Watch outOne subclass per variation multiplies quickly; when the choice is plain configuration, pass a factory function in instead.

2.09

Abstract Factory

Create a whole matching family of tools, such as shell and file system, for one environment, so local and sandboxed tools never mix.

Analogy

The theatre costume department

When the company stages Hamlet, the wardrobe pulls every cloak, crown and sword from the Elsinore rail. For next month's space opera, the same request for the prince's outfit returns a silver flight suit. Nobody walks on stage in a doublet with a laser pistol, because every piece comes from one production's rail.

Classic definition

Provide an interface for creating families of related objects without naming their concrete classes.

In the harness

A coding agent needs a shell, a file system tool and often a browser, and they must agree on where the workspace lives. A ToolkitFactory interface declares make_shell, make_fs and make_browser. LocalToolkit returns tools that act on the user's disk; SandboxToolkit returns tools that all target the same container and mounted volume. The session picks one factory from its environment setting, so a file written by the sandbox fs is always visible to the sandbox shell, and no code path can pair a local shell with a sandboxed file system.

How it flows
  1. The session reads its environment setting: local or sandbox.
  2. It selects the matching concrete toolkit factory.
  3. It calls make_shell, make_fs and make_browser on that one factory.
  4. The resulting family is registered and shares one workspace.
Sketch
class ToolkitFactory(Protocol):
    def make_shell(self): ...
    def make_fs(self): ...

class SandboxToolkit(ToolkitFactory):
    def __init__(self, box):
        self.box = box
    def make_shell(self):
        return ContainerShell(self.box)
    def make_fs(self):
        return VolumeFS(self.box.mount)

kit = KITS[session.env](env_handle)
tools = [kit.make_shell(), kit.make_fs()]

Watch outAdding a new kind of tool means changing every factory in the family, so keep the family small and stable.

2.10

Factory Kit

Build a frozen kit of named tool builders once at startup, then stamp out exactly the tool set each agent profile asks for.

Analogy

Surgical tray cards

The hospital's sterile supply room keeps a laminated card for every procedure. When the day's schedule says appendectomy, a technician reads that card and lays out exactly those instruments on a fresh tray. New cards are added by the head nurse, never by whoever is assembling trays at two in the morning.

Classic definition

A factory whose creatable types are configured up front, usually as a map from names to builder functions, and then made immutable.

In the harness

At startup the harness fills a ToolKit with builder functions: bash builds a sandboxed shell, grep builds a search tool, read builds a file reader rooted at the workspace. The kit is then frozen. Agent profiles such as reviewer.yaml list only names, and kit.create(['grep', 'read']) returns a fresh tool set for that subagent. Because the kit is closed after startup, no profile can reach a tool the operator did not install, and each subagent gets new instances instead of shared mutable ones.

How it flows
  1. The harness registers a builder function for each installable tool name.
  2. It freezes the kit so no names can be added at runtime.
  3. A subagent profile lists the tool names it needs.
  4. kit.create(names) calls each builder and returns a fresh tool set.
Sketch
kit = ToolKit()
kit.add('bash', lambda: Bash(box=sandbox))
kit.add('grep', lambda: Grep(root=repo))
kit.add('read', lambda: ReadFile(root=repo))
kit.freeze()

profile = load('agents/reviewer.yaml')
tools = kit.create(profile.tools)
# -> [Grep(...), ReadFile(...)]
kit.create(['curl'])  # raises UnknownTool

Watch outA builder that returns one shared object instead of a new instance lets subagents trample each other's state.

2.11

Builder

Assemble a large model request from system blocks, tools, history, cache breakpoints and limits piece by piece, then validate it once.

Analogy

The custom bicycle workshop

A frame builder does not hand you a bike in one go. You choose the frame size, then the gears, then the wheels, then the handlebars, and each part is clamped on in the work stand. Only when everything is fitted does the mechanic test the brakes and wheel it out the door.

Classic definition

Separate the construction of a complex object from its representation, so the same step-by-step process can produce different results.

In the harness

A single model request can hold a layered system prompt, dozens of tool schemas, a long message history, cache_control breakpoints, a thinking budget and max_tokens. A RequestBuilder lets the loop add these as they become known: system blocks from settings and memory files, tools from the registry, history from the transcript after compaction. build() then checks the whole request once: total tokens within the context window, cache breakpoints within the provider's limit, every tool_result paired with its tool_use. Subagent and eval variants reuse the same builder with different parts.

How it flows
  1. The loop creates a RequestBuilder for this turn.
  2. Settings, memory, registry and transcript each add their part.
  3. build() validates the token budget, cache breakpoints and tool pairing.
  4. The finished request is sent to the model API.
Sketch
req = (RequestBuilder(model=MODEL)
       .system(BASE_PROMPT)
       .system(memory.text(), cache=True)
       .tools(registry.schemas())
       .messages(transcript.compacted())
       .max_tokens(8000)
       .build())  # validates budget + pairs
resp = client.messages.create(**req)

Watch outIf build() does no validation, the builder is only a long constructor; put the cross-field checks there or skip the pattern.

2.12

Step Builder

Force a subagent or request spec through its required steps in a fixed order, so build() cannot be reached until each one is set.

Analogy

The airport check-in kiosk

The kiosk will not show seats until you scan a passport, and it will not print a bag tag until you have a seat. Each screen offers only the next button. You cannot walk away with a boarding pass that has no name on it, because no screen ever let you skip the name.

Classic definition

A builder variant where each step returns a type exposing only the next valid step, so the type system enforces order and completeness.

In the harness

Spawning a subagent needs a model, a system prompt, a tool set and a token budget, and a forgotten budget means a runaway run. A SubagentSpec step builder starts with a ModelStep that has only .model(), which returns a PromptStep with only .system(), then a ToolsStep with only .tools(), then a BudgetStep with only .budget(). Only the final BuildStep offers optional extras and .build(). A type checker flags a missing step before the harness runs, and the order matches how specs are reviewed: model, instructions, capabilities, limits.

How it flows
  1. SubagentSpec.new() returns a ModelStep that exposes only .model().
  2. Each call returns the next step type: prompt, then tools, then budget.
  3. Only the final BuildStep has .build(), alongside optional extras.
  4. A skipped step shows up as a type error before anything runs.
Sketch
spec = (SubagentSpec.new()
        .model('fast-model')
        .system(REVIEW_PROMPT)
        .tools(['grep', 'read'])
        .budget(tokens=50_000)
        .build())

class ModelStep:
    def model(self, m) -> 'PromptStep':
        return PromptStep(m)
# ModelStep has no .build(): skipping fails

Watch outA step builder adds one class per step, so keep it for specs where a missing field is dangerous, not for every options object.

2.13

Prototype

Clone a tuned agent or tool configuration template and change only a few fields, instead of building each variant from scratch.

Analogy

The tailor's sample suit

A tailor keeps a sample jacket on the rail that has already been fitted, pinned and tested. For a new customer they copy its pattern and change only the sleeve length and the cloth. The sample stays on the rail untouched, ready to be copied again.

Classic definition

Create new objects by copying an existing prototype instance and then adjusting the copy.

In the harness

A well-tuned code reviewer subagent carries a long system prompt, a curated tool list, a model choice, stop rules and hooks. When the orchestrator fans reviewers out over several directories, it deep-copies the reviewer template and sets only the directory scope and output file on each copy. Because every clone keeps the template's prompt prefix byte for byte, the copies also share the prompt cache. The template itself is never mutated, so the next fan-out starts from the same known state.

How it flows
  1. The harness loads a named template such as reviewer from the template store.
  2. The orchestrator deep-copies it once per task.
  3. Each copy gets its own small overrides, such as scope and output path.
  4. The copies are spawned as subagents while the template stays unchanged.
Sketch
base = templates.get('reviewer')

def variant(scope):
    spec = copy.deepcopy(base)
    spec.scope = scope
    spec.output = f'reviews/{scope}.md'
    return spec

specs = [variant(d) for d in
         ['api/', 'web/', 'db/']]
for s in specs: harness.spawn(s)

Watch outA shallow copy shares nested lists such as tools or hooks, so one variant's edit leaks into the template and its siblings; always deep-copy.

2.14

Proxy

Put a permission and sandbox layer with the same interface in front of every real tool, so nothing executes without passing its checks.

Analogy

The bank teller's window

Customers never walk into the vault. They speak to a teller behind glass who checks their ID, their balance and the withdrawal limit, and calls a manager for a large amount. Only then does the teller go to the vault and come back with cash. To the customer the window works just like the vault, only safer.

Classic definition

Provide a surrogate object with the same interface as the real one, so it can control access to it.

In the harness

Every tool in the registry is wrapped in a GuardedTool proxy that exposes the same run(args) as the real tool. Before forwarding, the proxy evaluates allow and deny rules for the tool name and arguments (bash commands matching rm -rf, writes outside the workspace), shows an approval card when no rule decides, and runs the real call inside the sandbox with a timeout. On the way back it redacts secrets and logs the decision to the transcript. The agent loop cannot tell the difference, and there is no path to the real tool that skips the proxy.

How it flows
  1. The loop calls run(args) on the proxy exactly as it would on the real tool.
  2. The proxy checks allow and deny rules against the tool name and arguments.
  3. If no rule decides, it pauses for user approval in the UI.
  4. Once allowed, it forwards the call into the sandbox, then redacts and logs the result.
Sketch
class GuardedTool(Tool):
    def __init__(self, real, policy, ui):
        self.real, self.policy = real, policy
        self.ui, self.name = ui, real.name
    def run(self, args):
        v = self.policy.check(self.name, args)
        if v == 'ask':
            v = self.ui.approve(self.name, args)
        if v != 'allow':
            return ToolResult.denied(v)
        out = sandbox.run(self.real, args)
        return redact(out)

Watch outA proxy only guards what it wraps; a tool registered without it, or a raw subprocess call elsewhere in the harness, is an open side door.

2.15

Virtual Proxy

Stand in for an expensive tool with a light stub, and load its full schema or start its server only when it is first needed.

Analogy

The library's closed stacks

The catalogue lists a rare atlas with a shelf mark and a one-line description, but the atlas itself sits in a basement store. Only when a reader hands in a request slip does a porter bring it up to the reading room. After that it stays on the desk for the day, and nobody fetches it twice.

Classic definition

A proxy that delays creating or loading an expensive object until a client actually uses it.

In the harness

A session may have hundreds of MCP tools available, and putting every full JSON schema in the system prompt would cost tens of thousands of tokens and start servers that are never used. Instead the harness registers a stub per tool holding only its name and a one-line description. When the model first selects a deferred tool, through a tool search call or directly, the stub starts the MCP server, fetches the full schema, appends it to the context and swaps in the real adapter. Later calls go straight through.

How it flows
  1. The system prompt lists deferred tools by name and one-line description only.
  2. The model selects a deferred tool for the first time.
  3. The stub starts its server, fetches the full schema and appends it to the context.
  4. The stub keeps the real tool, so later calls skip the loading step.
Sketch
class LazyTool(Tool):
    def __init__(self, name, desc, loader):
        self.name, self.desc = name, desc
        self._load, self._real = loader, None
    def real(self):
        if self._real is None:
            self._real = self._load()
            ctx.add_schema(self._real.spec)
        return self._real
    def run(self, args):
        return self.real().run(args)

Watch outLoading a schema mid-session changes the prompt, so append new schemas after the cached prefix instead of reordering the tool list.

2.16

Dynamic Proxy

Generate callable tool stubs at runtime from JSON schemas, routing every call through one generic invocation handler.

Analogy

The learning universal remote

You point the old TV remote at a learning universal remote and press each button once. The universal remote now shows a button for every function it heard, though nobody wired those buttons by hand. Whichever one you press, the same transmitter inside sends the matching code to the right device.

Classic definition

A proxy created at runtime for a given interface, where every method call is dispatched to a single invocation handler.

In the harness

When an MCP server connects, it answers tools/list with names, descriptions and JSON input schemas, but the harness has no Python class for any of them. A proxy factory reads each schema and generates a stub on the fly: a callable with the right name, docstring and argument validation. Every stub forwards to one invoke handler that serialises the arguments into a tools/call request, sends it over the transport and maps the response back into a tool_result block. Connecting a new server adds new tools without writing or deploying any code.

How it flows
  1. The harness connects to an MCP server and requests tools/list.
  2. For each schema, a factory builds a stub with the tool's name and parameter validation.
  3. The stubs are registered and their schemas are offered to the model.
  4. When the model calls one, the stub hands the name and arguments to the shared handler, which sends tools/call and returns the result.
Sketch
def make_stub(client, s):
    def stub(**args):
        validate(args, s['inputSchema'])
        return client.call(s['name'], args)
    stub.__name__ = s['name']
    stub.__doc__ = s['description']
    return stub

for s in client.list_tools():
    tools[s['name']] = make_stub(client, s)

Watch outGenerated stubs trust whatever the server sends, so check tool names and descriptions against an allowlist before exposing them, or a hostile server can smuggle instructions to the model.

2.17

Decorator

Wrap a tool in layers such as logging, retries, rate limits and telemetry, each adding one behaviour behind the same interface.

Analogy

Layering up for the ski slope

A skier pulls on a thermal base layer, then a fleece, then a waterproof shell. Each layer adds one thing (warmth, insulation, weather protection) and each fits over whatever is underneath. The skier inside is the same person, and on a mild afternoon the fleece comes off without touching the other layers.

Classic definition

Attach extra responsibilities to an object dynamically by wrapping it in objects that share its interface and forward calls to it.

In the harness

The harness keeps tools as plain objects with a run(args) method and wraps each one when it builds the tool set. A Telemetry wrapper records a span and the call's cost, a Logged wrapper writes the call and result to the transcript, a Retry wrapper retries transient network errors with backoff, and a RateLimit wrapper waits for a slot before calling a paid API. Every wrapper exposes the same name and schema, so neither the model nor the executor can tell how many layers surround the real tool. Configuration chooses the stack per tool: a local file read might get only logging, while web search gets all four.

How it flows
  1. The registry loads the bare tool implementation.
  2. The builder wraps it in the configured decorators, innermost first.
  3. A call enters the outermost wrapper, which does its job and forwards inward.
  4. The result travels back out through each layer, which can record, transform or retry it.
Sketch
class Retry(Tool):
    def __init__(self, inner, n=3):
        self.inner, self.n = inner, n
        self.name = inner.name
    def run(self, args):
        for i in range(self.n):
            try: return self.inner.run(args)
            except Transient: sleep(2 ** i)
        raise ToolFailed(self.name)

t = Telemetry(Logged(Retry(RateLimit(web))))

Watch outOrder matters: a retry outside the rate limiter waits for a fresh slot on each attempt, while one inside it can burst past the limit, so define the stack order in one place.

2.18

Delegation

A tool hands the real work to a helper object or subagent and returns that answer as its own result.

Analogy

The general contractor's subcontractors

You hire one general contractor to redo your kitchen. They promise the whole job, but the wiring is done by an electrician and the tiling by a tiler they bring in. You never phone the electrician: the contractor checks the work and hands you one finished kitchen.

Classic definition

An object exposes a behaviour but forwards each request to a second object that implements it, composing behaviour instead of inheriting it.

In the harness

A research tool exposed to the model may contain no search logic at all: it holds a reference to a delegate and forwards the request. The heavier version delegates to a subagent: the tool spawns a fresh agent with its own context window, a narrowed tool set and a written brief, waits for its final report and returns that report as the tool_result. The main agent's context sees one call and one answer, not the dozens of tool calls the subagent made along the way. Swapping the delegate (a cheaper model, a different search backend) changes nothing for the caller.

How it flows
  1. The model calls a tool such as research(question).
  2. The tool writes a brief and passes it to its delegate, here a subagent with its own context.
  3. The delegate does the work with its own tools and returns a compact report.
  4. The tool returns that report as its tool_result, as if it had done the work itself.
Sketch
class ResearchTool(Tool):
    name = 'research'
    def __init__(self, spawn):
        self.spawn = spawn      # the delegate
    def run(self, args):
        sub = self.spawn('researcher',
                tools=['search', 'read'])
        report = sub.run(brief(args['q']))
        return report.summary

Watch outDelegation hides cost: a one-line tool call can start a subagent that spends thousands of tokens, so pass a token budget down and report usage back up.

2.19

Servant

Put shared chores like path sanitising or result truncation in one helper that many tools call, not a copy per tool.

Analogy

The air pump at the petrol station

No car comes with its own compressor. Drivers pull up to the one air pump on the forecourt, push the hose onto their tyre valve and set the pressure. The pump serves a hatchback, a van or a motorbike because each has the same standard valve, and no car is modified to use it.

Classic definition

A helper class that provides a common behaviour to a group of classes, which pass their data to it instead of implementing the behaviour themselves.

In the harness

Many tools need the same chores done to their inputs and outputs. A PathGuard servant resolves a requested path, follows symlinks and rejects anything outside the workspace root; read_file, write_file and grep all call it. A ResultTruncator servant trims long tool output to a token budget, keeps the head and tail, and appends a note telling the model how to page for more. Because tools hand their data to the servant rather than inheriting from a shared base class, the rule lives in one place and a security fix reaches every tool at once.

How it flows
  1. A tool receives arguments from the model, such as a file path.
  2. It passes the path to the PathGuard servant, which normalises and checks it.
  3. The tool does its own work with the safe path.
  4. It passes its raw output to the ResultTruncator servant before returning the tool_result.
Sketch
class PathGuard:                 # servant
    def __init__(self, root): self.root = root
    def safe(self, p):
        r = (self.root / p).resolve()
        if not r.is_relative_to(self.root):
            raise Denied(p)
        return r

def read_file(args, guard, trunc):
    p = guard.safe(args['path'])
    return trunc.fit(p.read_text(), 8000)

Watch outA servant that grows tool-specific branches (if tool == 'grep') has become a god object; keep it to the shared rule and let tools own their quirks.

2.20

Null Object

Supply a do-nothing collaborator when a capability is switched off, so the agent loop never branches on None.

Analogy

The tree in the school play

Every child in the school play has a part, even the ones who did not want a line. The third tree from the left stands in position, takes the same cues, bows at the end and says nothing. The director runs the show the same way whether that slot holds a speaking role or a tree.

Classic definition

Replace a null reference with an object that implements the expected interface but whose methods do nothing, removing null checks from callers.

In the harness

The agent loop calls many optional collaborators: a tracer, a memory store, a UI renderer, an approval prompter. When the agent runs headless in a scheduled task there is no chat UI, so the harness injects a NullRenderer whose on_token and on_tool_card methods do nothing. With long-term memory disabled, a NullMemory returns an empty recall list and accepts writes without storing them, and with no telemetry exporter a NullTracer hands out empty spans. The loop calls the same methods every time, with no if renderer is not None checks scattered through it.

How it flows
  1. At startup the harness reads configuration for each optional collaborator.
  2. Where one is disabled or missing, it injects the matching null implementation.
  3. The loop calls tracer, memory and renderer methods unconditionally.
  4. Null implementations return empty, neutral values and record nothing.
Sketch
class NullMemory(Memory):
    def recall(self, query): return []
    def remember(self, fact): pass

class NullTracer(Tracer):
    def span(self, name): return nullcontext()

mem = VectorMem(url) if url else NullMemory()
tr = OTelTracer() if otel else NullTracer()

Watch outNever hand the model a silent no-op tool: a write_file that quietly does nothing lets the agent believe it saved work, so leave missing tools out of the tool list instead.

2.21

Special Case

Return a dedicated result object for expected odd outcomes, like no matches or file not found, that carries its own sensible behaviour.

Analogy

The no-receipt returns policy

At a department store returns desk, a customer without a receipt is not turned away or treated as a fault. The till has a defined no-receipt path: store credit at the lowest recent price, with a note on the account. The clerk presses the same Refund button, and the special case already knows what a refund means for it.

Classic definition

A subclass that provides special behaviour for a particular case, such as an unknown customer, so callers need no conditional checks for it.

In the harness

Search and lookup tools hit predictable dead ends: grep finds nothing, a path does not exist, a ticket id is unknown. Instead of returning None or raising, the tool returns a special case object such as NoMatches or MissingFile that implements the same ToolResult interface. Its to_block() produces a useful tool_result for the model ('No matches for retry_cfg in 412 files; try a broader pattern'), it keeps is_error false because an empty search is a valid answer, and it costs only a few tokens. The executor, transcript and renderer treat it like any other result.

How it flows
  1. A lookup tool runs and finds nothing, or hits another expected odd condition.
  2. Instead of None or an exception, it returns a special case result object.
  3. The executor calls to_block() on it exactly as it would for real results.
  4. The model receives a short message with a suggested next step.
Sketch
class NoMatches(SearchResult):
    def __init__(self, pat, n):
        self.pat, self.n = pat, n
    def to_block(self):
        return text(
            f'No matches for {self.pat} in '
            f'{self.n} files. Try a broader '
            'pattern or check the spelling.')

hits = index.search(q)
return Hits(hits) if hits else NoMatches(q, n)

Watch outKeep special cases for expected situations; a disk error or a permission failure is a real error and should surface as one, not be dressed up as no results.

2.22

Extension Objects

Let harness components ask a tool at runtime for optional capabilities such as streaming, undo or preview, without widening every tool's interface.

Analogy

The stand mixer's attachment hub

A stand mixer has a covered port on its front. One kitchen fits a pasta roller there, another a mincer, most fit nothing at all. A recipe that needs mincing first checks whether the mincer is attached and, if not, tells the cook to chop by hand; the mixer itself stays the same machine.

Classic definition

Add interfaces to an object without changing its class by letting clients request named extension objects that implement the extra behaviour.

In the harness

Every tool implements a small core interface (name, schema, run), but some can do more: a shell tool can stream output line by line, an edit tool can show a diff preview before applying and keep an undo record after, a browser tool can return a screenshot. Rather than adding stream(), preview() and undo() to every tool, the harness asks tool.get_extension('preview') and receives either an object implementing Previewable or None. The approval card shows a diff when a preview exists and the raw arguments when it does not, and the streaming renderer subscribes only to tools that return a Streaming extension.

How it flows
  1. Each tool registers the extension objects it supports under capability names.
  2. A harness component asks the tool for the extension it needs.
  3. If one comes back, the component uses its richer interface.
  4. If not, the component falls back to the plain run() path.
Sketch
class EditTool(Tool):
    def __init__(self):
        self.ext = {'preview': DiffPreview(),
                    'undo': EditUndo()}
    def get_extension(self, name):
        return self.ext.get(name)

pv = tool.get_extension('preview')
if pv: ui.show_diff(pv.render(args))
else:  ui.show_args(args)

Watch outIf every tool ends up implementing the same extension, promote it to the core interface; extension lookups are for capabilities that are truly optional.

2.23

Marker Interface

Tag tools as read-only, destructive or approval-required with empty markers that the permission gate checks before execution.

Analogy

Hazard placards on lorries

A tanker carries an orange placard with a number on it. The placard does not change how the lorry drives, but at the tunnel entrance the officer reads it and sends flammable loads the long way round. One small sign, checked by someone else, decides the route.

Classic definition
