An empty interface (or attribute) with no methods that marks a class as having some property other code can test for.

In the harness

Tool classes inherit from empty marker types such as ReadOnly, Destructive or NeedsApproval, or carry equivalent flags like readOnlyHint and destructiveHint in an MCP tool's annotations. The markers add no methods. The permission gate checks them before each call: read-only tools run immediately even in plan mode, destructive ones pause for user approval, and network tools are blocked in an offline sandbox. The scheduler reads the same tags to run read-only calls in parallel and serialise anything that writes.

How it flows
  1. Each tool declares its markers when it is defined.
  2. The model emits a tool_use block naming some tool.
  3. The permission gate checks the tool's markers against the session's mode.
  4. It runs the call, asks the user, or refuses it, without knowing what the tool actually does.
Sketch
class ReadOnly: pass       # markers carry
class Destructive: pass    # no methods

class ListDir(Tool, ReadOnly): ...
class DeleteFile(Tool, Destructive): ...

def gate(tool, mode):
    if isinstance(tool, Destructive):
        return 'ask'
    if isinstance(tool, ReadOnly):
        return 'run'
    return 'run' if mode == 'auto' else 'ask'

Watch outA marker is only a claim by the tool's author; treat hints on third-party MCP tools as untrusted and keep your own policy list for them.

2.24

Type Object

Define each tool as a data record (name, schema, handler) instead of a new class, so adding a tool adds no code.

Analogy

Creature cards in a game expansion

When a board game publishes an expansion, it does not rewrite the rulebook. It prints new creature cards: name, speed, strength, special ability. Every miniature on the board points to its card, and the same rules read whatever the card says.

Classic definition

Represent a family of types as instances of a single class, so new types can be added as data at runtime instead of as subclasses.

In the harness

An MCP tool definition is a type object: a JSON record with name, description, inputSchema and annotations, and every server's tools are instances of one ToolDef type rather than distinct classes. The harness has one generic ToolCall class whose instances point at their ToolDef for validation and display, the way a miniature points at its card. Teams add tools by editing a JSON or YAML file that maps a definition to an existing handler (an HTTP endpoint, a shell template, an MCP call), and the harness loads them at startup. Settings shared by every call of a type, such as default timeout and cost class, live on the definition.

How it flows
  1. Definitions are loaded from JSON, YAML or a tools/list response into ToolDef instances.
  2. Each ToolDef names a generic handler and holds the schema and shared settings.
  3. When the model calls a tool, the harness creates a ToolCall that references its ToolDef.
  4. Validation, timeouts and rendering read from the ToolDef rather than from a subclass.
Sketch
class ToolDef:             # the type object
    def __init__(self, d):
        self.name = d['name']
        self.schema = d['inputSchema']
        self.timeout = d.get('timeout', 30)
        self.handler = HANDLERS[d['handler']]

class ToolCall:            # an instance
    def __init__(self, tdef, args):
        validate(args, tdef.schema)
        self.tdef, self.args = tdef, args

Watch outData-defined tools are only as safe as the handlers they can point at, so keep the handler table small and reviewed rather than letting config reach arbitrary code.

2.25

Bytecode

Have the model write a short program in a constrained action language that a harness VM verifies and runs step by step.

Analogy

The player piano roll

A player piano reads a paper roll punched with holes. Each hole can mean only one thing: press this key, hold this pedal. Anyone can punch a new roll and the piano will play it, but no roll, however strange, can make the piano do anything except play notes.

Classic definition

Encode behaviour as instructions for a small virtual machine, so behaviour can be defined as data and executed safely within fixed limits.

In the harness

Instead of giving the model a general shell, the harness defines a tiny action language for browsing: OPEN url, FIND selector, CLICK ref, TYPE ref text, EXTRACT field. The model writes a short program as a JSON list of instructions inside one tool_use, and a harness VM verifies it (known opcodes only, operand types, at most 50 steps, allowed domains) before running it with a program counter and step budget. Because the instruction set has no opcode for arbitrary code, file deletion or new hosts, the worst program is a useless one. Batching ten steps into one program also saves nine model round trips.

How it flows
  1. The tool schema describes the opcodes and their operands to the model.
  2. The model returns a program: an ordered list of instructions.
  3. The verifier rejects unknown opcodes, bad operands, disallowed hosts or programs over the step limit.
  4. The VM executes one instruction at a time, stops at the first failure and returns a trace.
Sketch
OPS = {'OPEN': op_open, 'CLICK': op_click,
       'TYPE': op_type, 'EXTRACT': op_extract}

def run(program, limit=50):
    verify(program, OPS, limit)   # first
    trace = []
    for pc, ins in enumerate(program):
        out = OPS[ins['op']](*ins['args'])
        trace.append((pc, ins['op'], out))
        if out.failed: break
    return trace

Watch outEvery opcode you add widens what a model, or a prompt injection, can make the VM do; an EVAL or SHELL opcode turns the design back into arbitrary code.

2.26

Abstract Document

Keep tool call metadata in one flexible key-value document, with small typed views that read only the properties each component needs.

Analogy

The auction lot sheet

Every lot at an auction house gets the same kind of sheet, but the fields vary: a painting has artist and dimensions, a ring has carat and metal, a car has mileage. The shipper reads weight and size, the insurer reads the valuation, the catalogue writer reads provenance. Each reads its own fields from the one sheet.

Classic definition

Store an object's properties in a map and expose them through small typed interfaces (traits), so new properties need no schema change.

In the harness

A tool call gathers metadata from many places: the model's input, MCP annotations, harness settings (timeout, cost class), UI hints (icon, display title) and audit fields added on the way (approved_by, duration_ms). Rather than one class with dozens of optional attributes, the harness keeps them in a single dict-backed document with nested child documents. Small typed views such as HasTimeout, HasApproval and HasDisplay give each component accessors over the same dict, so the executor, the permission gate and the tool card renderer read only what they understand. Unknown keys from a newer MCP server pass through to the transcript untouched.

How it flows
  1. The harness builds a call document from the tool_use input plus definition metadata.
  2. Components add properties as the call moves through the pipeline.
  3. Each component reads through its own typed view of the document.
  4. The whole document is written to the transcript, including keys no view knows about.
Sketch
class Document(dict):
    def child(self, k):
        return Document(self.get(k, {}))

class HasTimeout(Document):
    def timeout(self):
        return self.get('timeout_s', 30)

class HasApproval(Document):
    def approver(self):
        return self.get('approved_by')

class CallDoc(HasTimeout, HasApproval): pass

Watch outA schemaless bag lets typos ('timout_s') fail silently, so give each view a defaults table and log any key that no view ever reads.

2.27

Property

Give each tool a property map that falls back to a parent map, so tools inherit defaults and override only what differs.

Analogy

Table limits at a casino

Each blackjack table posts a small sign with its own minimum and maximum bets. Anything not on the sign follows the casino's house rules, and anything the house rules leave out follows the state gaming regulations. When the casino changes a house rule overnight, every table without its own sign follows it the next morning.

Classic definition

Objects keep their properties in a map and delegate lookups for missing keys to a parent object, forming a prototype chain.

In the harness

Tools share many settings: timeout, retry count, output token cap, sandbox profile, approval mode. The harness keeps a root property map of defaults, a child map per MCP server (a slow remote server sets timeout_s to 120) and a map per tool holding only its own differences. A lookup such as tool.get('timeout_s') walks from the tool to its server to the root and returns the first value it finds. Changing a root default updates every tool that has not overridden it, and a subagent's tool set can be a child map that overrides only approval_mode.

How it flows
  1. The harness creates a root map of default tool properties.
  2. Each MCP server or tool family gets a child map that points to the root.
  3. Each tool gets its own map with only its overrides, pointing to its family.
  4. A lookup checks the tool, then each parent in turn, and returns the first value found.
Sketch
class Props:
    def __init__(self, parent=None, **own):
        self.parent, self.own = parent, own
    def get(self, k):
        if k in self.own: return self.own[k]
        return self.parent.get(k)

root = Props(timeout_s=30, approval='ask')
remote = Props(root, timeout_s=120)
fetch = Props(remote, approval='auto')
fetch.get('timeout_s')    # 120, from remote

Watch outDeep chains make 'why is this timeout 120?' hard to answer, so keep the chain short and have the tool inspector show which level supplied each value.

2.28

Parameter Object

Bundle a tool's many arguments into one typed request object that is validated once and passed along whole.

Analogy

The photo lab order envelope

At a photo lab you do not shout instructions across the counter. You fill in one envelope (print size, gloss or matte, copies, crop, name and phone) and drop the film inside. The envelope travels with the job from counter to machine to pickup shelf, and everyone who handles it reads the same fields.

Classic definition

Replace a group of parameters that always travel together with a single object, giving the group a name, validation and defaults.

In the harness

A run_command tool can take a command, working directory, environment, timeout, stdin, sandbox profile and output limit. Passing seven loose arguments through the permission gate, the sandbox and the executor invites mix-ups, so the harness parses the tool_use input once into a typed ShellRequest (a dataclass or Pydantic model built from the same JSON schema the model sees). Validation and defaults happen in one place, the gate checks req.command and req.cwd, and the transcript stores the request whole. Adding a field later changes the request class, not every function signature along the path.

How it flows
  1. The model emits tool_use input as a JSON object.
  2. The harness parses it into a typed request, filling defaults and rejecting bad fields.
  3. The gate, sandbox and executor each receive the one request object.
  4. The same object is logged with the result, so the call can be replayed exactly.
Sketch
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ShellRequest:
    command: str
    cwd: Path = Path('.')
    timeout_s: int = 60
    env: dict = field(default_factory=dict)
    max_output: int = 30_000

req = ShellRequest(**block.input)
gate.check(req)
result = sandbox.run(req)

Watch outDo not let one request class become a grab bag shared by unrelated tools; one request type per tool keeps the schema the model sees honest.

2.29

Execute Around

Run every tool body inside a function that sets up the sandbox first and always tears it down afterwards, even on failure.

Analogy

The cleanroom airlock

In a chip factory, an engineer cannot simply walk onto the floor. The airlock gowns them and runs an air shower, then lets them work, and on the way out it takes the gown back and logs the time. The procedure is the same whatever job they came to do, and nobody skips the exit half.

Classic definition

A method performs setup and cleanup around a block of code passed in by the caller, so callers cannot forget either half.

In the harness

Running a code tool needs a scratch directory, a container or VM slice, mounted workspace files, a network policy and CPU and wall-clock limits; afterwards the container must be killed, temp files deleted and logs collected. The harness exposes one context manager, sandbox(profile), that does all of that and runs the tool's body in the middle. Tool authors write only the body. A crash, a timeout or the user pressing stop still reaches the finally block, so orphaned containers do not pile up between turns.

How it flows
  1. The executor enters sandbox(profile) and passes control to the tool body.
  2. The wrapper starts the container, mounts files and applies limits.
  3. The body runs its command inside the sandbox and returns or raises.
  4. Either way, the finally block collects logs, kills the container and deletes temp files.
Sketch
@contextmanager
def sandbox(profile):
    box = containers.start(profile)
    box.mount(workspace, ro=profile.ro)
    try:
        yield box
    finally:
        box.collect_logs(transcript)
        box.kill(); box.cleanup()

with sandbox(DEFAULT) as box:
    out = box.exec(req.command, timeout=60)

Watch outTeardown cannot rely on the body behaving: enforce wall-clock limits from a watchdog outside the sandbox, because a hung body never returns control to the finally block.

2.30

Fluent Interface

Configure an agent with chained method calls that read like a sentence, each returning the builder for the next call.

Analogy

The sandwich counter in one breath

'Rye, turkey, swiss, toasted, cut in half, to go.' Each word passes the same half-built sandwich down the counter to the next station, and 'to go' is the moment it gets wrapped and handed over. Leave out a word and you get the house default; ask for something impossible and the counter tells you before wrapping.

Classic definition

An API built on method chaining, where each call returns an object supporting the next, so code reads as a small domain-specific sentence.

In the harness

Agent SDKs often offer a fluent configuration API: Agent('reviewer').model(...).system(...).tools(read, grep).max_turns(20).on_tool_use(audit).build(). Each method records one setting and returns the builder, so a whole agent definition fits in one readable expression that reviews cleanly in a pull request. The final build() validates the combination (a shell tool has a sandbox, the token budget fits the model's context window) and returns an immutable AgentConfig. Subagent definitions start from a shared base chain and add a few calls.

How it flows
  1. Start a builder with the agent's name.
  2. Chain calls for model, system prompt, tools, limits and hooks; each returns the builder.
  3. Call build() to validate the whole configuration at once.
  4. Hand the immutable config to the harness to start runs.
Sketch
class Agent:
    def model(self, m):
        self.cfg['model'] = m
        return self          # enables chaining

cfg = (Agent('reviewer')
       .model('large')
       .system(load('review.md'))
       .tools(read_file, grep, git_diff)
       .max_turns(20)
       .build())           # validates once

Watch outChains hide intermediate state, so a setting given twice or in a conflicting order can silently win; make build() reject contradictions instead of keeping the last call.

03
Chapter 3 · Talking to the LLM

The Model Call Layer

The model is a remote, rate-limited, sometimes-failing, metered service that returns imperfect text. The patterns here keep calls flowing: routing, retrying, failing over, caching, metering and reading messy output without crashing.

GatewayAmbassadorBridgeRetryFallbackCircuit BreakerRate LimitingThrottlingLoad SheddingBackpressureQueue-Based Load LevelingCachingObject PoolMultitonSingletonTolerant ReaderPartial ResponseMoney
3.01

Gateway

Route every model call through one client that holds credentials, picks a provider and fails over when one is down.

Analogy

The alliance check-in desk

At a big airport, partner airlines share one check-in desk. You show your passport once, and the agent books you onto whichever partner has a seat on your route. If one carrier cancels, the same desk rebooks you on another without you queuing again. You never deal with the airlines one by one.

Classic definition

An object that encapsulates access to an external system or resource behind a single, simple interface.

In the harness

The agent loop never imports a provider SDK. It calls gateway.complete(request), and the gateway attaches API keys from the secret store, maps the request to the provider's wire format, and routes it by model alias, region or tenant policy. It also records usage and latency for every call in one place. When a provider returns errors or is marked unhealthy, the gateway sends the same request to the next configured route and returns a normalised response, so subagents and scheduled tasks all get the same behaviour.

How it flows
  1. An agent or subagent calls gateway.complete with messages, tools and a model alias.
  2. The gateway resolves the alias to a list of provider routes and attaches credentials.
  3. It encodes the request in that provider's format and sends it.
  4. If the provider is down, it marks it unhealthy and tries the next route.
  5. It returns one normalised response with usage attached.
Sketch
class ModelGateway:
    def complete(self, req):
        for p in self.routes[req.model]:
            if not p.healthy():
                continue
            try:
                r = p.send(req, self.keys)
                self.meter.record(r.usage)
                return p.decode(r)
            except ProviderDown:
                p.mark_down()
        raise NoProviderAvailable(req.model)

Watch outA gateway that silently fails over to a weaker model can change agent behaviour mid-task, so log every reroute and record which model actually answered.

3.02

Ambassador

Run a sidecar beside the harness that owns the model connection, handling credentials, TLS, retries, timeouts and telemetry.

Analogy

The reporter's local fixer

A foreign correspondent arriving in a new city hires a fixer who goes everywhere with them. The reporter says who they want to interview; the fixer handles permits, translation, phone lines that drop and checkpoints that want paperwork. The reporter's notebook holds only the story, and a fixer who knows a different city can be swapped in without changing the reporter's job.

Classic definition

A helper service deployed alongside a client that sends network requests on its behalf, adding connectivity features such as retries, monitoring and security.

In the harness

The harness process sends plain HTTP to a sidecar on localhost instead of calling the provider directly. The sidecar runs in the same pod or container group, holds the API key, terminates TLS, adds retries with backoff, enforces timeouts and emits metrics and traces for every model call. Because it is language-agnostic, a Python agent worker and a TypeScript UI server share one connection policy. Rotating keys or changing egress rules means redeploying the sidecar, not the agent code.

How it flows
  1. The harness posts a model request to the sidecar on localhost.
  2. The sidecar adds the API key, a timeout and a trace id.
  3. It forwards the request to the provider over TLS and retries transient failures.
  4. It streams the response back and emits latency and token metrics.
Sketch
# harness: no keys, no retry logic
client = ModelClient(
    base_url='http://localhost:8787')
resp = client.messages.create(**req)

# ambassador sidecar, same pod
@app.post('/v1/messages')
async def relay(req):
    req.headers['x-api-key'] = vault.key()
    return await retry(upstream.post, req,
                       timeout=60)

Watch outIf both the harness and the ambassador retry, one failure becomes many calls; decide which side owns retries and turn them off on the other.

3.03

Bridge

Keep the family of agent types separate from the family of model backends, so either side can grow without multiplying classes.

Analogy

The universal remote

A universal remote comes in a basic model with volume and channel, and a deluxe one that also records and pauses. Separately, every television brand speaks its own infrared codes. Any remote can drive any brand because it holds a code set for the TV it is paired with. Nobody manufactures a 'deluxe remote for brand X'.

Classic definition

Decouple an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently, joined by a reference from one hierarchy to the other.

In the harness

The agent side has its own hierarchy: ChatAgent, CodingAgent and ResearchAgent differ in system prompt, tools and loop policy. The backend side has another: a hosted API backend, a cloud-platform backend and a local inference backend, each knowing its own request format, streaming quirks and auth. Each agent holds a reference to a ModelBackend and calls only its narrow interface (generate, stream, count_tokens). Three agents and three backends need six classes instead of nine combinations, and a new backend works with every agent on day one.

How it flows
  1. Define a narrow ModelBackend interface: generate, stream and count_tokens.
  2. Implement one backend class per provider or deployment.
  3. Write agent classes against that interface and inject a backend at construction.
  4. Choose the pairing in config, for example CodingAgent with a local backend in tests.
Sketch
class Agent:                 # abstraction
    def __init__(self, backend):
        self.backend = backend

class CodingAgent(Agent):
    def step(self, msgs):
        return self.backend.generate(
            CODE_PROMPT, msgs, TOOLS)

class LocalBackend(ModelBackend): ...
class HostedBackend(ModelBackend): ...

agent = CodingAgent(LocalBackend())

Watch outKeep the backend interface to what every provider can honour; leaking one provider's special feature into it quietly turns the bridge into a single-provider adapter.

3.04

Retry

Re-send a model call that failed for a transient reason, waiting longer each time, and give up after a fixed budget.

Analogy

The radio phone-in competition

When a radio station opens its prize line, thousands dial at once and most hear the engaged tone. If everyone redials instantly, the line stays jammed. Callers who wait a few seconds, then a little longer, each picking a slightly different moment, get through. After ten tries, sensible people stop and listen to the rest of the show.

Classic definition

Transparently repeat an operation that failed due to a transient fault, usually with an increasing delay, until it succeeds or a limit is reached.

In the harness

Model APIs return transient errors: 429 when a rate limit is hit, 529 or 503 when the service is overloaded, and occasional 500s or connections dropped mid-stream. The harness's model client catches these, reads any retry-after header, and sleeps with exponential backoff plus random jitter before resending the identical request. Errors that can never succeed on a resend, such as 400 invalid_request or 401 authentication, fail immediately. The budget is bounded by attempts and by the turn's deadline, so a user in the chat is never left waiting indefinitely.

How it flows
  1. The client sends the request and receives a 529 overloaded error.
  2. It classifies the error as transient and computes a delay of base times two to the power of the attempt, plus jitter.
  3. If the response carries retry-after, it waits at least that long.
  4. It resends the same request, up to the maximum number of attempts.
  5. It returns the first success, or raises the last error to the agent loop.
Sketch
RETRYABLE = {429, 500, 503, 529}
for attempt in range(MAX_TRIES):
    try:
        return api.create(**req)
    except APIError as e:
        if e.status not in RETRYABLE:
            raise
        wait = BASE * 2 ** attempt
        wait += random.uniform(0, wait)
        sleep(max(wait, e.retry_after or 0))
raise GaveUp(req)

Watch outRetries stacked at several layers (SDK, gateway, agent loop) multiply into dozens of calls during an outage; retry in exactly one place.

3.05

Fallback

When the preferred model cannot answer, hand the same request to a substitute so the turn still completes, perhaps with lower quality.

Analogy

The understudy in the wings

Every lead role in a theatre production has an understudy who knows the lines. If the star loses their voice an hour before curtain, a slip goes into the programme and the understudy goes on. The audience still sees the show, a little differently. Nobody cancels the night because one actor is out.

Classic definition

Provide an alternative action or result when the primary operation fails, so the system degrades gracefully instead of erroring.

In the harness

After retries are exhausted or a circuit breaker is open, the model client walks a fallback chain: the same model in another region, then a smaller model, then a canned 'busy, try again' reply. Each step gets the identical messages and tool definitions, adjusted only where the substitute needs it (a smaller max_tokens, no extended thinking). The response is tagged with the model that actually served it, so the transcript, cost accounting and evals stay honest. Some callers, such as a review subagent that must use the strongest model, opt out and fail loudly instead.

How it flows
  1. Call the primary model with the request.
  2. On exhausted retries or an open breaker, pick the next entry in the fallback chain.
  3. Adapt the request to the substitute's limits and send it.
  4. Tag the response with served_by and return it to the agent loop.
Sketch
CHAIN = ['large', 'large-eu', 'small']

def complete(req):
    for model in CHAIN:
        try:
            r = call(model, fit(req, model))
            r.served_by = model
            return r
        except (Overloaded, BreakerOpen):
            continue
    return canned_reply('busy, try later')

Watch outA fallback model may not support the same tools, context length or output format, so run the agent's evals against every model in the chain.

3.06

Circuit Breaker

Stop calling a provider that keeps failing, fail fast for a cool-down period, then let one trial call decide whether to resume.

Analogy

The harbour master's storm flag

When three ferries in a row turn back in a gale, the harbour master raises the storm flag and stops all sailings, and passengers are told at the gate instead of halfway out to sea. After a few hours she sends one boat out to test the water. If it crosses safely the timetable resumes; if not, the flag goes back up.

Classic definition

Wrap calls to a remote service in a state machine that opens after repeated failures, rejects calls while open, and probes with a trial call before closing again.

In the harness

The model client keeps one breaker per provider, or per model and region. While closed, calls flow normally and failures are counted in a rolling window. When 5xx or 529 errors cross a threshold, the breaker opens: for the next 30 seconds every call fails instantly with BreakerOpen, which the fallback layer turns into a switch to another model, and no agent burns its retry budget on a dead endpoint. After the cool-down the breaker goes half-open and lets one probe request through; success closes it, failure re-opens it with a longer timer.

How it flows
  1. Closed: requests pass through and the breaker counts recent failures.
  2. Open: once the threshold is crossed, calls fail immediately for a cool-down period.
  3. Half-open: when the timer expires, one trial request is allowed through.
  4. The trial's result closes the breaker or opens it again.
Sketch
def call(self, req):
    if self.state == 'open':
        if now() < self.retry_at:
            raise BreakerOpen(self.provider)
        self.state = 'half_open'
    try:
        r = self.provider.send(req)
    except ServerError:
        self.fail()   # may open again
        raise
    self.state, self.fails = 'closed', 0
    return r

Watch outCount only provider-side failures; tripping the breaker on 400s caused by a malformed prompt takes a healthy provider offline for every agent.

3.07

Rate Limiting

Cap how many requests and tokens each caller may spend per window, rejecting the excess with a clear time to retry.

Analogy

Timed tickets at the museum

A blockbuster exhibition sells entry in half-hour slots of fifty people. When the 2:00 slot is full, the fifty-first visitor is told the next free slot is 2:30. Everyone inside gets a calm look at the paintings, and the people turned away know exactly when to come back.

Classic definition

Restrict the number of operations a client may perform in a time window, rejecting or deferring requests above the limit.

In the harness

Providers already enforce limits on requests per minute and input and output tokens per minute, answering 429 with a retry-after header. A multi-tenant harness adds its own limiter in front, usually a token bucket per organisation or per user, so one user's runaway agent loop cannot exhaust the shared provider quota. The limiter charges the estimated input tokens plus the max_tokens reservation before the call and settles real usage afterwards. A request that would overdraw the bucket is rejected at once with the time until enough tokens refill.

How it flows
  1. Estimate the request's input tokens and add the max_tokens reservation.
  2. Refill the caller's bucket for the elapsed time and check its balance.
  3. If it has room, deduct and forward the call; otherwise return 429 with retry_after.
  4. After the response, refund or charge the difference against actual usage.
Sketch
class TokenBucket:
    def take(self, n):
        self.refill(now())
        if self.tokens < n:
            need = n - self.tokens
            raise RateLimited(need/self.rate)
        self.tokens -= n

bucket = buckets[req.org_id]
bucket.take(estimate(req) + req.max_tokens)

Watch outBad token estimates make the limiter useless or unfair, so reconcile against the usage the provider reports after every call.

3.08

Throttling

Slow callers to a sustainable pace by spacing out model calls, so the harness stays under its limits instead of being rejected.

Analogy

Ramp meters on the motorway

At rush hour a traffic light on the slip road lets one car onto the motorway every few seconds. Every car gets on eventually; the queue on the ramp absorbs the surge so the main carriageway keeps moving. When traffic thins, the light turns green and stays green.

Classic definition

Control the rate at which a consumer uses a resource by delaying or degrading service when demand exceeds a threshold, rather than failing outright.

In the harness

When rate-limit headers show remaining requests and tokens shrinking, or occasional 429s appear, the harness throttles itself before the provider starts rejecting. A shared pacer spaces out model calls from all running agents, lowers how many subagents may run concurrently, or downgrades background work (shorter max_tokens, no extended thinking). Interactive turns still go through, a little later. As headroom recovers, the pacer shortens its interval.

How it flows
  1. Read the rate-limit headers after each model call.
  2. Compute a minimum gap between calls from the remaining budget and reset time.
  3. Before each new call, wait until that gap has passed.
  4. Shorten the gap as headroom returns.
Sketch
class Pacer:
    def adjust(self, h):
        left = int(h['tokens-remaining'])
        reset = float(h['tokens-reset'])
        self.gap = reset / max(left / AVG, 1)

    async def wait_turn(self):
        due = self.last + self.gap
        await sleep(max(0, due - now()))
        self.last = now()

Watch outThrottling only hides overload up to a point; if the ramp queue grows without bound you also need load shedding or backpressure.

3.09

Load Shedding

When demand exceeds capacity, drop or defer the least important model work so interactive turns keep getting answered.

Analogy

Rolling cuts on a heatwave grid

On the hottest afternoon of the year, demand outruns the power stations. Rather than let the whole grid collapse, the operator cuts supply to a few industrial estates for an hour. Hospitals, homes and traffic lights stay on, and the cut is announced in advance and reversed when demand falls.

Classic definition

Deliberately reject a portion of incoming requests, chosen by priority, when a system is overloaded, to protect its core function.

In the harness

Each model request carries a priority: a user waiting in the chat UI is high, a subagent on a background task is medium, and scheduled digests, eval runs and memory consolidation are low. When provider errors rise, queue depth or p95 latency crosses a threshold, or the org's token budget is nearly gone, the admission check rejects calls below the current cut-off with a 'shed' status and defers them to a later scheduled task. Interactive turns keep their latency, and shed work is recorded so it can run when load drops.

How it flows
  1. Tag every model request with a priority class.
  2. Measure load: queue depth, latency, provider errors and remaining budget.
  3. Above a threshold, reject or defer requests below the current cut-off priority.
  4. Record shed work and lower the cut-off as load recovers.
Sketch
PRIORITY = {'chat': 3, 'subagent': 2,
            'eval': 1, 'digest': 0}

def admit(req):
    cutoff = 0
    if load.p95_ms > 8000: cutoff = 2
    elif load.queue > 200: cutoff = 1
    if PRIORITY[req.kind] < cutoff:
        deferred.put(req)   # run later
        raise Shed(req.kind)
    return dispatch(req)

Watch outShedding must be visible: a background job that is silently dropped every afternoon looks like a bug, so surface deferrals in logs and job status.

3.10

Backpressure

Let a slow consumer push back on its producer, so work waits at the source instead of piling up in memory.

Analogy

The sushi conveyor belt

At a conveyor sushi bar the chef places a plate only where the belt has a gap. When diners are slow and the belt is full, there is nowhere to put the next plate, so the chef pauses and waits. As diners lift plates off, gaps appear and the chef starts again. The belt never overflows onto the floor.

Classic definition

A flow-control mechanism where a downstream component signals its capacity upstream, causing producers to slow or pause when buffers fill.

In the harness

An orchestrator fanning out subagents puts each task into a bounded queue; when every model-call slot in the dispatcher is busy, queue.put blocks and the orchestrator stops spawning, so memory stays flat however many tasks the model plans. Streaming works the same way: if a mobile chat client renders slowly, the server reads the next server-sent event only after the websocket buffer drains, and the pause propagates back through TCP to the provider. The slowest stage sets the pace for the whole chain.

How it flows
  1. Connect producer and consumer with a bounded buffer.
  2. The consumer drains the buffer at its own pace.
  3. When the buffer is full, the producer's put or write awaits.
  4. Freed space releases the producer and flow resumes.
Sketch
q = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=8)

async def orchestrator(plan):
    for task in plan.subtasks:
        await q.put(task)   # waits when full

async def dispatcher():
    while True:
        task = await q.get()
        await run_subagent(task)
        q.task_done()

Watch outAn unbounded queue anywhere in the chain defeats backpressure, because the producer never feels the push and memory grows until the process dies.

3.11

Queue-Based Load Leveling

Put model jobs in a durable queue drained by a fixed pool of workers, so bursts become a steady, affordable call rate.

Analogy

The reservoir behind the dam

A storm dumps a week's rain on the hills in one night. The river below would flood, but the reservoir fills instead. The sluice gates release water at a steady rate the town's channels can carry, day after day, until the level falls.

Classic definition

Use a queue as a buffer between tasks and a service so intermittent heavy loads are smoothed, letting the service process work at its own consistent rate.

In the harness

At 9am hundreds of scheduled tasks fire at once, and a CI webhook can launch fifty review agents in a minute. Instead of each calling the model immediately, the harness writes a job record to a durable queue and returns a run id. A worker pool sized to the provider's sustained rate limit pulls jobs and runs the agent loop, so the provider sees a flat line of traffic and the 429s disappear. Callers watch run status or get a completion notification, and nothing is lost if a worker restarts.

How it flows
  1. Producers (schedules, webhooks, users) enqueue a job and get a run id.
  2. The queue stores jobs durably and absorbs the burst.
  3. A fixed pool of workers pulls jobs at a rate matched to the model budget.
  4. Each worker runs the agent and posts the result and a notification.
Sketch
def on_webhook(event):
    run_id = new_id()
    jobs.enqueue({'run': run_id,
                  'agent': 'pr_review',
                  'pr': event.pr})
    return {'run_id': run_id}   # at once

def worker():                    # N of these
    while job := jobs.dequeue(block=True):
        result = run_agent(job)
        notify(job['run'], result)

Watch outLoad leveling trades latency for stability; a user waiting in the chat should not sit behind a thousand batch jobs, so give interactive work its own lane.

3.12

Caching

Reuse work already paid for: cache the stable prompt prefix with the provider and memoise deterministic tool results locally.

Analogy

The library's reserve shelf

In exam season the same twenty textbooks are requested all day. Instead of sending a porter to the basement stacks each time, the librarian keeps copies on a reserve shelf behind the desk. Those requests are answered in seconds, anything else still goes to the stacks, and the shelf is refreshed when the reading list changes.

Classic definition

Store the results of expensive operations so that repeated requests for the same data are served from fast storage instead of recomputed.

In the harness

Every turn re-sends the tool definitions, system prompt and earlier conversation. Marking the end of that stable prefix with a cache_control breakpoint lets the provider reuse its processed state, so later calls report cache_read_input_tokens at a fraction of the normal price and with lower latency; the entry expires after a few minutes without use. Locally, the harness memoises deterministic, read-only tool calls (fetching the same URL, reading an unchanged file) keyed by tool name, arguments and a content hash. Anything with side effects or time-sensitive data bypasses the cache.

How it flows
  1. Order the prompt so tools and system text come first and rarely change.
  2. Place a cache breakpoint after the stable prefix.
  3. On the next call the provider matches the prefix and bills cached reads.
  4. For tool calls, look up the key locally before executing and store the result after.
Sketch
system = [{'type': 'text', 'text': RULES,
           'cache_control':
               {'type': 'ephemeral'}}]

@memo(key=lambda a: (a['url'], day()))
def fetch_page(a):
    return http.get(a['url']).text

r = client.messages.create(model=M,
    system=system, tools=TOOLS, messages=h)
log(r.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)

Watch outA timestamp or random id near the top of the system prompt changes the prefix on every call and silently turns every cache read into a full-price write.

3.13

Object Pool

Keep expensive resources such as sandboxes, browsers and connections warm, lending them to agents and resetting them on return.

Analogy

Bowling shoes at the lanes

A bowling alley does not make a new pair of shoes for every customer. You give your size, borrow a pair from the rack, bowl, and hand them back. Staff spray and dry each pair before it returns to the shelf, and if the rack is empty you wait a few minutes for a pair to come back.

Classic definition

Manage a set of initialised, reusable objects that clients borrow and return, avoiding the cost of repeated creation and destruction.

In the harness

Starting a code sandbox container or a headless browser takes seconds, and opening a fresh TLS connection to the model API on every call adds latency. The harness keeps pools: a few warm sandboxes, a browser pool for web tools, and the HTTP client's keep-alive connection pool. An agent checks out a sandbox for a bash or code-execution tool call; on return the pool wipes the working directory, kills stray processes and resets environment variables before lending it again. When every instance is busy, callers wait with a timeout or the pool grows up to a hard cap.

How it flows
  1. At startup, create N warm instances and put them on the idle list.
  2. A tool call acquires an instance, waiting if none is idle.
  3. The tool runs inside the borrowed instance.
  4. On release the pool resets it and returns it to the idle list, or destroys it if the reset fails.
Sketch
class SandboxPool:
    def acquire(self, timeout=30):
        sb = self.idle.get(timeout=timeout)
        return Lease(sb, self.release)
    def release(self, sb):
        try:
            sb.reset()  # wipe fs, procs, env
            self.idle.put(sb)
        except ResetFailed:
            sb.destroy(); self.spawn_one()

with pool.acquire() as sb:
    out = sb.run(tool_input['command'])

Watch outA resource returned dirty leaks one session's files or cookies into another user's agent, so treat reset as security-critical and destroy anything that fails it.

3.14

Multiton

Keep exactly one client per key, such as provider and model or tenant, created on first use and shared afterwards.

Analogy

Embassy row in the capital

A capital city has one embassy per country. Ask a taxi for the French embassy and you always arrive at the same building. When a new country is recognised, its embassy opens, and from then on that is the one. There is never a second French embassy across town issuing different visas.

Classic definition

Like a Singleton, but manages a map of named instances, guaranteeing one instance per key.

In the harness

Each provider and model combination needs its own client with its own base URL, credentials, connection pool and rate-limit tracker. ModelClient.get(provider, model) returns the existing instance for that key or builds one on first use, under a lock so two concurrent subagents do not both build it. Every agent asking for the same key shares one connection pool and one view of remaining quota, while another tenant's key gets an isolated client with its own API key.

How it flows
  1. A caller asks for the client keyed by provider and model, or by tenant.
  2. The class looks the key up in its instance map.
  3. On a miss it builds the client under a lock and stores it.
  4. Every later caller with that key receives the same instance.
Sketch
class ModelClient:
    _all = {}
    _lock = threading.Lock()

    @classmethod
    def get(cls, provider, model):
        key = (provider, model)
        with cls._lock:
            if key not in cls._all:
                cls._all[key] = cls(*key)
            return cls._all[key]

Watch outA key that includes a volatile value, such as a per-request timeout, creates a new instance per call and quietly turns the multiton into a memory leak.

3.15

Singleton

Share one process-wide model client and settings object, so every agent uses the same connection pool, credentials and limits.

Analogy

One conductor for the orchestra

Eighty musicians watch the same baton. If a second conductor stood up beside the first and beat a slightly different tempo, half the strings would follow one and half the other. There is one podium and one person on it, and everyone knows where to look.

Classic definition

Ensure a class has only one instance and provide a global point of access to it.

In the harness

A harness process usually creates one SDK client at startup and shares it across the agent loop, subagents and background workers. That instance owns the HTTP connection pool, the API key, default timeouts and the retry policy. If each subagent built its own, the process would open redundant connections and each copy would track rate limits separately. Settings loaded from environment and config files are exposed the same way: get_settings() returns one cached object.

How it flows
  1. On first access, build the client from settings and cache it at module level.
  2. Every later call returns the cached instance.
  3. All agents and workers share its connection pool and retry policy.
  4. Tests replace it through an explicit override hook.
Sketch
from functools import cache

@cache
def get_settings():
    return Settings.from_env()

@cache
def get_client():
    s = get_settings()
    return ModelClient(api_key=s.api_key,
                       max_retries=s.retries,
                       timeout=s.timeout)

Watch outA singleton is global mutable state in disguise; inject it into agents instead of calling get_client() deep inside tools, or tests cannot swap in a fake.

3.16

Tolerant Reader

Parse model output by taking what you need and ignoring the rest, repairing small defects instead of crashing on them.

Analogy

The examiner marking messy scripts

An experienced examiner marking a maths paper looks for the answer and the key steps. Crossed-out working, arrows in the margin and a doodle in the corner do not cost marks. She only stops and flags a script when the answer itself is missing or unreadable.

Classic definition

A consumer reads only the parts of a message it needs and tolerates unknown fields, reordering and minor variations, so it survives changes by the producer.

In the harness

A model asked for JSON sometimes wraps it in a markdown fence, adds a sentence before it, leaves a trailing comma, returns numbers as strings or invents an extra field. A tolerant reader in the harness strips fences, extracts the first balanced object, applies a lenient repair, then reads only the required fields and coerces simple types, ignoring unknown keys. Structured verdicts from grader models and plans from planner subagents are read this way. Only when a required field is truly missing does the harness send a short corrective message back to the model.

How it flows
  1. Strip code fences and leading prose from the raw model text.
  2. Extract the first balanced JSON object and repair trivial syntax errors.
  3. Read the required fields, coerce simple types and ignore extra keys.
  4. If a required field is absent, ask the model for a corrected answer.
Sketch
def read_verdict(text):
    raw = strip_fences(text)
    obj = repair_json(first_obj(raw))
    # take what we need, ignore the rest
    return Verdict(
        score=int(obj['score']),   # '7' ok
        reason=obj.get('reason', ''))

try:
    v = read_verdict(reply.text)
except (KeyError, ValueError):
    ask_model_to_fix(reply)

Watch outTolerance belongs at the parsing edge only; pass strict typed objects inward, and never 'repair' inputs that authorise a destructive tool action.

3.17

Partial Response

Deliver a model's answer piece by piece as it is generated, or only the fields a caller asked for.

Analogy

Election night, seat by seat

On election night the television studio does not wait until dawn to read out every result at once. Each constituency is announced the moment its count finishes, so viewers watch the map fill in through the night and can go to bed early. Anyone who only wants the headline watches the strip at the bottom of the screen, which shows seat totals and nothing else.

Classic definition

Let a client receive part of a resource, either a subset of fields or a progressive stream of the result, to save bandwidth and latency.

In the harness

With streaming on, the model API sends server-sent events: message_start, then for each content block a content_block_start, a run of content_block_delta events carrying text_delta or input_json_delta fragments, and content_block_stop, then a message_delta with stop_reason and usage. The harness forwards text deltas to the chat UI immediately, buffers input_json_delta pieces until a tool_use block is complete before executing it, and can cancel the stream when the user presses stop. Field selection is the same idea for reads: a status endpoint polled by the UI returns only the run's state and token count, never the whole transcript.

How it flows
  1. Open a streaming request to the model API.
  2. Forward each text delta to the UI and append it to the turn buffer.
  3. Accumulate tool input fragments until the block stops, then parse and run the tool.
  4. On message_delta, record stop_reason and usage and close the turn.
Sketch
with client.messages.stream(**req) as s:
    for ev in s:
        if ev.type == 'content_block_delta':
            d = ev.delta
            if d.type == 'text_delta':
                ui.send(d.text)
            elif d.type == 'input_json_delta':
                js[ev.index] += d.partial_json
        elif ev.type == 'content_block_stop':
            maybe_run_tool(js, ev.index)

Watch outNever act on a partial tool input: a half-streamed path such as '/home/user/pro' is a valid prefix of the argument and the wrong file.

3.18

Money

Represent tokens and cost as typed amounts with a unit or currency, so arithmetic, budgets and reports cannot mix incompatible numbers.

Analogy

The bureau de change counter

At a currency exchange desk, nobody writes down just '100'. It is always 100 euros or 100 yen, and the clerk will not add the two without looking up today's rate first. Rounding happens once, at the end, to the smallest coin of the currency being paid out.

Classic definition

Model a monetary amount as a value object combining a quantity and a currency, with arithmetic that enforces currency rules and correct rounding.

In the harness

A response's usage block reports input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens, each priced differently per model. As bare integers they invite bugs: adding output tokens to input tokens, or summing a large model's tokens with a small model's as if they cost the same. The harness keeps Tokens(n, kind, model) and Money(micros, 'USD') value objects, converts through an explicit price table, and does arithmetic in integer micro-units. Budgets for a session, a subagent tree or a tenant are Money too, so a check like spent + estimate > budget is type-safe.

How it flows
  1. Read the usage block from each model response.
  2. Wrap each count as Tokens with its kind and model.
  3. Convert to Money using the price table for that model and kind.
  4. Add to the session ledger and compare against the Money budget.
Sketch
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Money:
    micros: int          # 1e-6 of a unit
    cur: str = 'USD'
    def __add__(self, o):
        assert o.cur == self.cur
        return Money(self.micros + o.micros,
                     self.cur)

def cost(u, model):
    p = PRICES[model]    # micros per token
    return Money(u.input_tokens * p.inp
                 + u.output_tokens * p.out)

Watch outFloating-point dollars drift after millions of tiny per-call charges; store integer micro-units and round only when displaying or invoicing.

04
Chapter 4 · What the agent remembers

Context and Memory

A context window is small and expensive; transcripts, files and memories are large and durable. These patterns decide what is stored, how it is loaded, how duplicates are avoided and how concurrent edits are kept safe.

RepositoryDAODAO FactoryData MapperDTOValue ObjectComposite EntityUnit of WorkIdentity MapLazy LoadingFlyweightWrite-Ahead LogEvent SourcingDirty FlagSerialized EntitySerialized LOBMetadata MappingSingle Table InheritanceTable InheritanceOptimistic Offline LockVersion NumberShardingClient SessionServer Session
4.01

Repository

Give the agent's memory a collection-like interface (add, search, remove) so loop code never touches the vector store or database directly.

Analogy

The library circulation desk

You ask the librarian for books on tide pools. She might pull them from the open shelves, the basement stacks or an inter-library loan, but you just get a pile of books handed over at the desk. You return them to the same desk, and she decides where each one goes.

Classic definition

Mediates between the domain and the data mapping layers through a collection-like interface for accessing domain objects.

In the harness

The agent loop asks a MemoryRepository for what is relevant to this turn: repo.search(query, k=5). Behind it might sit a vector store of embeddings, a SQL table of past conversations or a folder of markdown memory files. The repository speaks in domain objects (Memory, Turn), applies scoping such as user id and recency, and hides the embedding call. Swapping the vector store, or using an in-memory repository in evals, changes no loop code.

How it flows
  1. The loop builds a query from the latest user message.
  2. It calls repo.search(query, k) with the current user's scope.
  3. The repository embeds the query, queries its backend and maps hits to Memory objects.
  4. The loop renders those memories into the context window and saves new facts with repo.add().
Sketch
class MemoryRepo(Protocol):
    def add(self, m: Memory): ...
    def search(self, q, k=5) -> list: ...

class VectorMemoryRepo(MemoryRepo):
    def search(self, q, k=5):
        hits = self.index.query(embed(q),
                                top_k=k)
        return [Memory.from_hit(h)
                for h in hits]

mems = repo.search(user_msg, k=5)

Watch outDo not leak store-specific query syntax (filter dicts, SQL fragments) through the repository; once callers depend on it, the abstraction is gone.

4.02

DAOData Access Object

Wrap one storage backend's raw API in a small object with plain append, load and delete calls for one record type.

Analogy

The pharmacy counter

You hand a prescription across the counter and later collect a paper bag with your name on it. Behind the counter are drawers, a fridge and a filing system you never see. The pharmacist offers a few fixed actions (fill, collect, return), and the back room can be reorganised overnight without the counter changing.

Classic definition

An object that provides an abstract interface to a particular database or persistence mechanism, exposing data operations without revealing storage details.

In the harness

A TranscriptDAO gives the harness a handful of calls: append(session_id, message), load(session_id), list_sessions(user_id) and delete(session_id). Inside sit the SQL, the connection pool, the JSON encoding of content blocks and the paging through long transcripts. The session service and the memory repository call the DAO rather than the database driver, so moving transcripts from an embedded database file on a laptop to a managed SQL server in production touches one class.

How it flows
  1. The session service calls dao.append(sid, message) after each turn.
  2. The DAO encodes the content blocks to JSON and runs an INSERT through its pool.
  3. On resume, dao.load(sid) selects rows in sequence order.
  4. The DAO decodes each row back into a Message and returns the list.
Sketch
class TranscriptDAO:
    def __init__(self, db): self.db = db
    def append(self, sid, msg):
        self.db.execute(
          'INSERT INTO turns VALUES (?,?,?)',
          (sid, msg.seq, msg.to_json()))
    def load(self, sid):
        rows = self.db.query(
          'SELECT body FROM turns WHERE sid=?'
          ' ORDER BY seq', (sid,))
        return [Message.from_json(r)
                for r in rows]

Watch outA DAO that only mirrors SQL one-to-one adds little; keep its methods in harness terms (append a turn, load a session) and give each record type one DAO.

4.03

DAO Factory

Pick a storage backend once at startup and get a matching family of DAOs (transcripts, memories, artifacts) that all use it.

Analogy

The travel adapter kit

Before a trip you pick the kit for the country you are visiting. Every plug in the box fits that country's sockets: one for the laptop, one for the phone, one for the shaver. You never end up with one British plug and two European ones, because you chose the kit, not the plugs.

Classic definition

An abstract factory that returns a family of DAOs for one data source, so an application switches storage by choosing a different concrete factory.

In the harness

The harness reads its config at startup: local mode wants an embedded database and the local filesystem, cloud mode wants a managed SQL server and object storage, evals want everything in memory. One factory per mode returns transcripts(), memories() and artifacts(), all wired to the same backend and credentials. The session service asks the factory for DAOs and never branches on mode, so a laptop run, a hosted run and an eval run cannot end up mixing stores.

How it flows
  1. At startup the harness reads the deployment mode from config.
  2. It instantiates the matching concrete factory once.
  3. Services ask the factory for each DAO they need.
  4. Every DAO in the family shares the same connection, bucket and credentials.
Sketch
class DAOFactory(Protocol):
    def transcripts(self) -> TranscriptDAO:...
    def artifacts(self) -> ArtifactDAO: ...

class LocalFactory(DAOFactory):
    def transcripts(self):
        return FileTranscriptDAO(self.root)
    def artifacts(self):
        return FileArtifactDAO(self.root)

FACTORIES = {'local': LocalFactory,
             'cloud': CloudFactory,
             'eval': MemoryFactory}
f = FACTORIES[cfg.mode](cfg)   # once

Watch outIf only one backend will ever exist the factory is ceremony; introduce it when a second real backend arrives (in-memory eval fakes count).

4.04

Data Mapper

Keep domain objects like Memory and Turn ignorant of storage by putting a separate mapper between them and the store.

Analogy

The removal crew

Movers take your sofa, lamp and bookcase apart, wrap them, and pack them into numbered crates that fit the van and the warehouse racks. At the new house they unpack and rebuild everything. Your sofa never learns about crate numbers, and the warehouse never learns about your living room.

Classic definition

A layer of mappers that moves data between objects and a database while keeping them independent of each other and of the mapper itself.

In the harness

A Memory in the harness has text, source, created_at, importance and methods like is_stale(). The vector store wants an id, a float vector and a flat metadata dict of strings. A MemoryMapper converts one way (to_record: embed the text, flatten fields, stringify dates) and back (from_hit: parse metadata, attach the similarity score). The Memory class imports nothing from the store client, so it can be unit tested without a database and moved to a different store by rewriting only the mapper.

How it flows
  1. Domain code creates and changes Memory objects with no persistence calls.
  2. On save, the mapper turns each Memory into a record with a vector and flat metadata.
  3. On load, the mapper parses search hits and rebuilds Memory objects with scores.
  4. A change to the store schema is absorbed in the mapper alone.
Sketch
class MemoryMapper:
    def to_record(self, m: Memory):
        return {'id': m.id,
                'vector': embed(m.text),
                'meta': {
                    'text': m.text,
                    'src': m.source,
                    'ts': m.ts.isoformat()}}
    def from_hit(self, h) -> Memory:
        return Memory(id=h.id,
                      text=h.meta['text'],
                      source=h.meta['src'],
                      score=h.score)

Watch outA mapper roughly doubles the code compared with objects that save themselves; for a few flat records with no logic, that cost may not pay off.

4.05

DTOData Transfer Object

Pass plain, serialisable message objects between harness layers and processes, carrying data only and no behaviour.

Analogy

The shipping container

A steel box of standard size moves from ship to crane to train to lorry. None of them needs to know whether it holds sofas or bananas; they only need the right shape and a manifest on the door. Nothing inside the box does anything during the journey.

Classic definition

An object that carries data between processes or layers, reducing the number of calls and holding no business logic of its own.

In the harness

When the agent loop talks to a sandboxed tool runner in another process, or the server streams events to the chat client, it sends DTOs: ToolRequest {call_id, name, input}, ToolResult {call_id, content, is_error}, StreamEvent {type, delta}. They are frozen dataclasses that serialise to JSON and carry a schema version. Live domain objects such as a Session or a ToolCommand, which hold file handles and methods, never cross the wire; the harness copies the needed fields into a DTO at the boundary.

How it flows
  1. The loop copies a tool_use block's fields into a ToolRequest.
  2. The request is serialised to JSON and posted to the tool runner.
  3. The runner rebuilds the DTO, executes the tool and replies with a ToolResult.
  4. The loop maps the ToolResult into a tool_result content block.
Sketch
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ToolRequest:
    v: int          # schema version
    call_id: str
    name: str
    input: dict

req = ToolRequest(1, b.id, b.name, b.input)
r = http.post(RUNNER, json=asdict(req))
res = ToolResult(**r.json())

Watch outDo not let DTOs grow methods or hold live handles such as open files or clients, and version them, because the two sides of the wire deploy at different times.

4.06

Value Object

Treat content blocks, messages and token counts as immutable values compared by content, so they can be shared, hashed and cached safely.

Analogy

Paint colour chips

At the paint shop, two chips marked Harbour Blue 5015 are the same colour, whichever rack they came from. You never repaint a chip to get a new shade; you pick another chip. Because a chip never changes, you can pin it to the wall and trust it next month.

Classic definition

A small object whose equality depends on its values rather than its identity, and which never changes after it is created.

In the harness

TextBlock('hello'), a ToolUse block and TokenCount(input=1200, output=340) are value objects: frozen, with equality and hashing over their fields. The harness relies on this in several places: prompt-cache keys hash the exact prefix of blocks, deduplication compares blocks by value, and usage totals add TokenCount values to produce new ones instead of mutating a counter that two turns share. A block in an already-sent prefix must never change in place, or the cached prefix silently stops matching.

How it flows
  1. Blocks and counts are created frozen.
  2. Changing one means making a new copy with replace().
  3. Equal content gives equal hashes and therefore the same cache key.
  4. Arithmetic such as total + usage returns a new TokenCount.
Sketch
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TokenCount:
    input: int = 0
    output: int = 0
    def __add__(self, o):
        return TokenCount(
            self.input + o.input,
            self.output + o.output)

a, b = TextBlock('hello'), TextBlock('hello')
assert a == b and hash(a) == hash(b)
total = total + turn.usage   # new object

Watch outA frozen dataclass that holds a list is still mutable through that list; use tuples inside value objects and never give them ids.

4.07

Composite Entity

Load and save a whole session (messages, todos, tool state, read files) as one aggregate through a single root object.

Analogy

The hospital patient chart

A ward nurse does not fetch blood results from one office, the medication list from another and scan reports from a third. The patient's chart binder holds all of them. It travels with the patient between wards, and when the doctor signs off, the whole chart is filed together.

Classic definition

A coarse-grained entity that manages a graph of dependent objects, so clients load and persist the whole graph through one interface.

In the harness

A Session object is the root of an aggregate: messages, a todo list, tool state such as the shell's working directory, the set of files the agent has read, and permission grants for this session. The harness loads it with sessions.get(id) and saves it with sessions.save(s), and only the root has a public id. Parts are reached through the root (s.todos.add, s.messages.append), so resuming, forking or handing a session to a subagent moves one consistent snapshot instead of five loosely related rows.

How it flows
  1. A resume request arrives with a session id.
  2. The store loads the root and its dependent parts in one call.
  3. The loop changes parts only through the root during the turn.
  4. At turn end the whole aggregate is saved in one write.
Sketch
class Session:              # aggregate root
    def __init__(self, sid):
        self.id = sid
        self.messages: list[Message] = []
        self.todos = TodoList()
        self.tool_state = {'cwd': '/repo'}
        self.read_files: set[str] = set()

s = sessions.get(sid)
s.todos.add('run tests')
sessions.save(s)    # one write, whole graph

Watch outIf every save rewrites megabytes of transcript the aggregate is too big; keep append-heavy parts like messages in their own log and hold references in the root.

4.08

Unit of Work

Collect a turn's memory, todo and message writes, then commit them together at the turn boundary or roll them all back.

Analogy

The supermarket trolley

You walk the aisles dropping items into the trolley and putting some back as you change your mind. Nothing is yours until you reach the till and pay once for the lot. If the card is declined you leave the trolley, and the shop's stock is exactly as it was.

Classic definition

Maintains a list of objects affected by a business transaction and coordinates writing out the changes, and resolving conflicts, as one unit.

In the harness

During one agent turn the model might save two memories, update the todo list, write an artifact and append three messages. The harness registers each change with a TurnUnitOfWork instead of writing it immediately. When the turn ends cleanly, uow.commit() writes everything in one transaction; if the user cancels, a token limit is hit or a tool throws, uow.rollback() drops the pending writes. The stored session never shows half a turn, and a retried turn does not duplicate memories.

How it flows
  1. Opening a turn opens a unit of work.
  2. Each write is registered as new, dirty or deleted instead of being saved.
  3. If the turn completes, commit() writes all changes in one transaction.
  4. If it is interrupted or fails, rollback() discards them and the store is untouched.
Sketch
with TurnUnitOfWork(db) as uow:
    uow.register_new(Memory('likes tabs'))
    uow.register_dirty(session.todos)
    uow.register_new(assistant_msg)
    run_turn(session, uow)
# __exit__: commit() on success,
# rollback() on any exception

Watch outSide effects outside the store, such as a sent email or a git push, are not undone by rollback; gate or defer them separately.

4.09

Identity Map

Keep one in-memory object per document id while building context, so a file or memory retrieved twice enters the window once.

Analogy

The wedding seating plan

Cousin Ana is on the bride's list and on the groom's list. The planner checks her name against the seating chart before writing a place card, so Ana gets one seat and one meal, not two. When her dietary needs change, there is only one card to correct.

Classic definition

Ensures each object is loaded only once by keeping every loaded object in a map keyed by its identity and returning the existing one on later lookups.

In the harness

In one turn, vector search returns chunk doc-17#3, a grep tool hits the same region of the file, and a memory recall pulls it again. Without care the context window holds three copies, wasting tokens and suggesting to the model that the fact is emphasised. A per-turn identity map keyed by source and chunk id (or path and content hash) returns the already loaded object, and the context builder cites it as [2] instead of pasting it again. A file edited by a tool is also updated in one place.

How it flows
  1. Retrievers return keys such as doc-17#3.
  2. Each key is looked up in the identity map.
  3. On a miss the document is loaded once and stored in the map.
  4. On a hit the existing object and its citation number are reused.
Sketch
class IdentityMap:
    def __init__(self): self._m = {}
    def get(self, key, load):
        if key not in self._m:
            self._m[key] = load(key)
        return self._m[key]

idmap = IdentityMap()          # per turn
for hit in rag_hits + grep_hits:
    doc = idmap.get(hit.key, store.load)
    ctx.cite(doc)      # same doc, same [n]

Watch outScope the map to one turn or session; a long-lived global map keeps serving old file contents after the file changes on disk.

4.10

Lazy Loading

Put light stubs for tool schemas and file contents into context, and fetch the full thing only when the agent asks.

Analogy

The furniture showroom tag

The showroom floor shows one of each table and chair, each with a small tag giving an aisle and bin number. Nobody hauls every flat-pack box to the checkout. You note the tags for what you want, and only those boxes come down from the warehouse racks.

Classic definition

An object that does not hold all the data it needs but knows how to get it, deferring the load until the data is first used.

In the harness

A harness connected to 200 MCP tools does not paste every JSON schema into the request. It lists tool names with one-line descriptions, and when the model wants one it calls a tool search step that loads the full schema into the tools list for the next request. Files work the same way: context holds a FileRef with path, size and a summary, and the content is read only when the model calls read_file. This saves thousands of tokens per turn and keeps the cached prompt prefix small.

How it flows
  1. The request lists deferred tools by name and description only.
  2. The model calls a search step naming the tool it needs.
  3. The harness fetches that schema from the MCP server and adds it to tools.
  4. The model calls the real tool with valid arguments; other schemas are never loaded.
Sketch
class LazyTool:
    def __init__(self, name, blurb, server):
        self.name, self.blurb = name, blurb
        self._srv, self._schema = server, None
    @property
    def schema(self):
        if self._schema is None:  # first use
            self._schema = self._srv.fetch(
                self.name)
        return self._schema

Watch outEach lazy load costs a round trip, and a loop over lazy refs turns into N fetches; preload the few tools or files that nearly every turn uses.

4.11

Flyweight

Share one immutable copy of the system prompt and tool schemas across thousands of sessions, keeping only per-session state separate.

Analogy

Projected hymn lyrics

A cathedral used to print 600 hymn sheets for every service. Now one screen at the front shows the words to everyone. Each singer brings only what is theirs: which part they sing and where they stand.

Classic definition

Use sharing to support large numbers of fine-grained objects efficiently, splitting shared intrinsic state from per-object extrinsic state.

In the harness

A hosted harness may run 10,000 sessions with the same 8,000-token system prompt and 40 tool schemas. A flyweight factory interns that bundle by content hash: every session holds a reference to one frozen PromptBundle and stores only its own messages, user id and settings. The sharing pays off again at the API, because identical prefixes hit the prompt cache. Per-session details such as the user's name or today's date go after the shared prefix as extrinsic state.

How it flows
  1. On session start the harness hashes the prompt version and tool set.
  2. The factory returns the existing bundle for that hash or builds it once.
  3. The session stores a reference plus its own messages and settings.
  4. Each request sends the shared prefix followed by the session's own content.
Sketch
_bundles: dict[str, PromptBundle] = {}

def bundle_for(version, tools):
    key = hash_of(version, tools)
    if key not in _bundles:
        _bundles[key] = PromptBundle.build(
            version, tools)       # frozen
    return _bundles[key]

s = Session(user, bundle=bundle_for(v, t))

Watch outNever put per-user details into the shared bundle; a name leaked into the flyweight appears in every session and breaks the cache prefix.

4.12

Write-Ahead Log

Append each tool call to a durable log before running it, so a crashed run can recover exactly where it stopped.

Analogy

The ship's logbook

Before the officer of the watch changes course, the order goes in the logbook with the time. If the bridge loses power in a storm, the next officer reads the log and knows the heading, the speed and the last order given, even though the instruments were reset.

Classic definition

Record every change in an append-only log and flush it to durable storage before applying it, so state can be recovered after a crash by reading the log.

In the harness

Before the harness executes a tool call it appends a tool_use record to the session's JSONL transcript and fsyncs; when the tool returns, it appends the tool_result. If the process dies mid-turn, the harness reads the tail of the log on restart: a tool_use without a matching tool_result marks an interrupted call. It reruns the call if the tool is idempotent, or tells the model the call was interrupted, instead of silently losing it or running it twice.

How it flows
  1. The model emits a tool_use block.
  2. The harness appends it to the log and flushes to disk.
  3. Only then does the tool run, and its result is appended and flushed.
  4. On restart, unmatched tool_use entries in the tail are resolved before the loop continues.
Sketch
def run_tool(call):
    wal.append({'type': 'tool_use',
                'id': call.id,
                'in': call.input})
    wal.fsync()              # durable first
    out = tools[call.name](**call.input)
    wal.append({'type': 'tool_result',
                'id': call.id, 'out': out})
    wal.fsync()

def recover():
    return [e for e in wal.tail()
            if unmatched(e)]

Watch outFlushing on every streamed token is far too slow; log at message and tool boundaries, and remember the log does not make a non-idempotent tool safe to rerun.

4.13

Event Sourcing

Store a session as append-only events and rebuild any view of it (model context, chat UI, a fork) by replaying them.

Analogy

The chess score sheet

Club players write every move on a score sheet: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6. Nobody photographs the board. From the sheet you can rebuild the position at move 30, go back to move 12 to study a blunder, or start a new game from that position.

Classic definition

Persist an entity's state as the sequence of events that changed it, and derive the current state by replaying those events.

In the harness

The harness stores events such as user_message, assistant_message, tool_use, tool_result, compaction and rewind, never a mutable current context. The context sent to the model is a projection: replay the events, apply compaction summaries, drop rewound branches. The chat UI is another projection and a cost report a third. Rewinding to a checkpoint or forking a subagent from turn 12 means replaying up to event 12 into a new stream, and nothing in the original history is overwritten.

How it flows
  1. Every change is appended as an event; nothing is updated in place.
  2. To build the next request, the harness folds the events into a message list.
  3. Other readers fold the same events into their own views.
  4. Rewind and fork replay a prefix of the events into a new stream.
Sketch
events = store.read(session_id)

def project_context(events, upto=None):
    msgs = []
    for e in events[:upto]:
        if e.type == 'message':
            msgs.append(e.msg)
        elif e.type == 'compaction':
            msgs = [e.summary]
        elif e.type == 'rewind':
            msgs = msgs[:e.to]
    return msgs

Watch outReplaying thousands of events every turn gets slow; store periodic snapshots of the projected context and replay only the events after the latest one.

4.14

Dirty Flag

Mark a memory or summary as changed when its source changes, and re-embed or recompact only when that mark is set.

Analogy

The hotel make-up-room card

Housekeeping does not strip every bed every morning. Guests who want service hang the card on the door handle, and the cleaner only enters those rooms. Rooms without a card are skipped, and the card comes off once the room is done.

Classic definition

Track whether derived data is out of date with a flag set when its source changes, and recompute only when the flag is set and the result is needed.

In the harness

Re-embedding a memory file or regenerating a conversation summary costs model calls. The harness keeps a dirty flag, or a stored content hash, for each derived artefact: when a memory note is edited the file watcher sets embedding_dirty, and when new messages pass the summary point summary_dirty is set. Before each turn a refresh step recomputes only artefacts whose flag is set and clears it. A quiet session with no new content costs nothing extra, and the cached prompt prefix stays byte-identical.

How it flows
  1. A write to the source sets the flag.
  2. Before the derived value is needed, the harness checks the flag.
  3. If set, it recomputes the embedding or summary and clears the flag.
  4. If clear, it reuses the stored result with no model call.
Sketch
class MemoryNote:
    def __init__(self, text):
        self.text, self.vec = text, None
        self.dirty = True
    def edit(self, text):
        self.text, self.dirty = text, True
    def vector(self):
        if self.dirty:        # changed?
            self.vec = embed(self.text)
            self.dirty = False
        return self.vec

Watch outA missed set is worse than a wasted recompute: if any write path forgets the flag the agent works from a stale summary, so prefer content hashes where writes come from many places.

4.15

Serialized Entity

Snapshot a whole live object, such as an agent checkpoint, into one serialised blob that can be stored, shipped and restored elsewhere.

Analogy

Packing the tent

At the end of a camping trip you fold the tent, poles, pegs and fly into one bag. Nobody writes down where each peg was. At the next campsite you tip out the bag and pitch the same tent again.

Classic definition

Serialise an object graph to a stream such as JSON or bytes so it can be stored or sent, then deserialise it into an equivalent object later.

In the harness
