When a long-running agent pauses for approval, or a scheduled task hands work to a fresh worker, the harness serialises a Checkpoint: messages, todo list, tool state, the pending tool call, model settings and a schema version. The blob goes to object storage or into a queue message, and any worker can deserialise it and continue the loop. A run can wait hours for a human without holding a live process, and moving a session between machines is a file copy.

How it flows
  1. At a pause point the harness builds a Checkpoint from live state.
  2. It serialises it with a version number and compresses it.
  3. The blob is stored under the session's key.
  4. A later worker loads it, migrates old versions and resumes the loop.
Sketch
@dataclass
class Checkpoint:
    v: int
    messages: list
    todos: list
    pending_call: dict | None

blob = gzip(json.dumps(asdict(ckpt)))
blobs.put(f'ckpt/{sid}', blob)
# later, on any worker:
d = json.loads(gunzip(blobs.get(key)))
ckpt = Checkpoint(**migrate(d))

Watch outNever unpickle checkpoints from untrusted sources, and keep a version field with migrations, because yesterday's blob must still load in today's code.

4.16

Serialized LOB

Store a transcript or artifact body as one serialised blob column in a row whose other columns stay small and queryable.

Analogy

The post office parcel

The counter clerk weighs your parcel and writes the postcode, weight and sender on the label. Sorting machines route it using only the label. Nobody opens the box until it reaches the person it is addressed to.

Classic definition

Save a graph of objects by serialising it into a single large object (LOB) in one database field, next to ordinary columns.

In the harness

The sessions table has id, user_id, title, model, updated_at and token_total as normal columns, plus a body column holding the compressed JSON of every message and content block. Listing a user's recent sessions or summing tokens per day reads only the small columns. The full blob is read when someone opens the session, and the harness never needs a table for each content block type (text, tool_use, image, citation).

How it flows
  1. On save, the harness copies index fields into their own columns.
  2. It serialises the message list to JSON, compresses it and writes it to the body column.
  3. List views select only the small columns.
  4. Opening a session selects and deserialises the body.
Sketch
db.execute(
    'INSERT INTO sessions(id, user_id,'
    ' title, tokens, updated, body)'
    ' VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?)',
    (s.id, s.user, s.title, s.tokens,
     now(), gzip(json.dumps(s.messages))))

recent = db.query(
    'SELECT id, title FROM sessions'
    ' WHERE user_id=? LIMIT 20', (uid,))

Watch outYou cannot query inside the blob efficiently (for example, every session that called the deploy tool); copy any field you filter on into its own column or a side index.

4.17

Metadata Mapping

Describe how memory records map to store fields in one declarative table, and let generic code do every load and save.

Analogy

The airport baggage hall

The conveyor system knows nothing about skis, prams or suitcases. It reads one routing table: flight 117 goes to belt 4, flight 220 to belt 7. When a new route opens, someone adds a line to the table, and nobody rewires the conveyor.

Classic definition

Hold the details of object-to-storage mapping in metadata, and use generic code that reads that metadata to load and save objects.

In the harness

A harness may keep memories, artifacts and scheduled tasks across a vector store and a SQL table. Instead of a hand-written mapper for each type, each record class declares a mapping: field text goes to meta.body, user_id goes to meta.uid as a filter key, vector is computed from text by the embedder. One generic save() and load() walk that map. Adding a field means adding a line, and the same metadata can generate the store schema and the list of filters exposed to a memory search tool.

How it flows
  1. Each record type declares its field mapping as data.
  2. Generic save() walks the mapping, converting and placing each field.
  3. Generic load() walks it in reverse to rebuild the object.
  4. Schemas and search filters are generated from the same mapping.
Sketch
MEMORY_MAP = [
    Field('id',   to='id'),
    Field('text', to='meta.body'),
    Field('user', to='meta.uid', filter=True),
    Field('text', to='vector', via=embed),
]

def save(obj, mapping, store):
    rec = {}
    for f in mapping:
        val = f.convert(getattr(obj, f.name))
        put(rec, f.to, val)
    store.upsert(rec)

Watch outMetadata hides behaviour: when a field silently stops persisting the bug lives in a table nobody reads as code, so validate the mapping at startup.

4.18

Single Table Inheritance

Persist every transcript event type in one table with a kind column, leaving the fields a type does not use empty.

Analogy

The lost property ledger

At a busy railway station every found item goes into one big ledger. There is a column for the kind of item and columns for colour, brand, size and screen type. An umbrella leaves screen type blank, a phone leaves size blank, and one book covers everything found.

Classic definition

Represent a class hierarchy as one table with columns for the fields of every class, plus a discriminator column naming each row's class.

In the harness

A transcript holds many entry types: UserMessage, AssistantMessage, ToolUse, ToolResult, Compaction, PermissionDecision. With single table inheritance they all live in one events table: session_id, seq, kind, plus nullable columns text, tool_name, tool_input, is_error and summary. Loading a session is one ordered SELECT on (session_id, seq), and the loader picks the class from kind. Queries across every type, such as everything in session 42 after seq 300, need no joins.

How it flows
  1. Each event type writes into the same table, setting kind and its own columns.
  2. Columns other types use are left NULL.
  3. Loading a session is a single ordered query.
  4. The loader maps each row's kind to the right class.
Sketch
ROW_CLASS = {'user': UserMsg,
             'tool_use': ToolUse,
             'tool_result': ToolResult,
             'compaction': Compaction}

rows = db.query(
    'SELECT * FROM events WHERE sid=?'
    ' ORDER BY seq', (sid,))
events = [ROW_CLASS[r['kind']].from_row(r)
          for r in rows]

Watch outEvery new type adds sparse columns, and the table cannot require tool_name only when kind is tool_use; add CHECK constraints, or move to table inheritance when types diverge a lot.

4.19

Table Inheritance

Keep fields shared by all events in a base table and each type's own fields in a separate table joined by event id.

Analogy

The vet clinic file

Every animal gets the same front card: name, owner, weight and visit date. Behind it the vet staples a species sheet: a dog's lists vaccinations and microchip, a parrot's lists wing clipping and beak checks. Reception reads only the front cards, and the vet pulls the sheet for the animal on the table.

Classic definition

Represent a class hierarchy with one table per class, where each subclass table holds only its own fields and shares the base table's primary key.

In the harness

Agent events share id, session_id, seq, created_at and tokens, stored in a base events table. Each type gets its own table keyed by the same id: tool_calls(id, tool, input, duration_ms, exit_code), approvals(id, decision, reviewer), compactions(id, summary, dropped_tokens). Timeline and cost queries read only the base table, while tool analytics join events to tool_calls and get NOT NULL constraints and an index on tool.

How it flows
  1. Writing an event inserts a base row and a row in its type's table with the same id.
  2. Cross-type queries such as cost per session read only the base table.
  3. Type-specific queries join the base table to one subtype table.
  4. Each subtype table enforces its own constraints.
Sketch
class Event(Base):        # table: events
    id: int; sid: str; seq: int; tokens: int
class ToolCall(Event):    # table: tool_calls
    tool: str; input: dict; exit_code: int
class Approval(Event):    # table: approvals
    decision: str; reviewer: str

slow = db.query(
    'SELECT e.sid, t.tool FROM events e'
    ' JOIN tool_calls t USING (id)'
    ' WHERE t.duration_ms > 30000')

Watch outLoading a full mixed transcript needs a join or a query per subtype, so this layout suits audit and analytics better than the hot path of resuming a session.

4.20

Optimistic Offline Lock

Let the agent and a person edit one document without locks, and detect at save time whether someone changed it first.

Analogy

The theatre box office

You look at the seating plan, think it over with a coffee, and come back to buy row F seat 12. Nobody held the seat for you. At the till the clerk checks it is still free; if someone bought it meanwhile, you are shown the current plan and choose again.

Classic definition

Prevent conflicts between concurrent business transactions by detecting a conflict at commit time and rejecting the stale write, instead of locking while people work.

In the harness

An agent reads an artifact (a doc, a spec, a config file) at the start of a long turn and spends a minute planning edits while the user types in the same doc. When the agent saves, the harness sends the version it read; the store compares it with the current version and rejects the write if it moved. The harness fetches the newer content, has the model rebase its edit onto it or runs a three-way merge, and saves again. Nothing was locked while the model thought, so the person was never blocked.

How it flows
  1. The agent reads the document and remembers its version.
  2. It works on edits with no lock held.
  3. It saves with expected_version; the store rejects the save if the version moved.
  4. On conflict it fetches the latest, merges its change and saves again.
Sketch
doc = store.get(doc_id)       # text + version
new = agent.edit(doc.text)
try:
    store.save(doc_id, new,
               expected=doc.version)
except VersionConflict as c:
    merged = merge3(doc.text, new,
                    c.current.text)
    store.save(doc_id, merged,
               expected=c.current.version)

Watch outOptimism suits rare conflicts; if the agent and a person collide on most saves, split the document or hand editing over explicitly instead of merging again and again.

4.21

Version Number

Stamp every stored artifact, memory and session with a counter that each write increments, so stale reads and writes are detectable.

Analogy

Revision stamps on building drawings

Every architect's drawing has a box in the corner reading Rev A, Rev B, Rev C. On site the foreman checks the drawing in hand against the latest revision before pouring concrete. A change request marked against Rev B when Rev D is current goes straight back to the office.

Classic definition

Store a version number on each record that increases with every update, used to detect stale data and to implement optimistic locking.

In the harness

Every artifact, memory file and session row carries an integer version. Writes are compare-and-set: UPDATE ... SET body = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?, and zero rows updated means someone else wrote first. The number also tags derived data: an embedding, a summary or a cached render records which version it was built from, so the harness knows when to rebuild, and the UI can tell the user the doc changed since the agent last read it.

How it flows
  1. Every reader receives the version along with the content.
  2. Every writer sends the version it read with its update.
  3. The database applies the update only if the version still matches, then increments it.
  4. Zero rows updated tells the writer its copy is stale.
Sketch
def save(art, body):
    n = db.execute(
        'UPDATE artifacts SET body=?,'
        ' version=version+1'
        ' WHERE id=? AND version=?',
        (body, art.id, art.version))
    if n == 0:
        raise StaleVersion(art.id)
    art.version += 1

Watch outTimestamps are a poor substitute: two writes in the same millisecond or clock skew between workers defeat them, so use an integer the database increments.

4.22

Sharding

Split session and memory stores by tenant, so each shard holds one slice of the data and each turn touches one shard.

Analogy

Conference registration desks

At a 5,000-person conference the badge desks are split by surname: A to F, G to M, N to S, T to Z. Each desk keeps only its own box of badges, so its queue moves quickly. You walk straight to your desk, and a crowd at one desk never slows the others.

Classic definition

Partition data horizontally across several databases by a shard key, so each database stores and serves a subset of the rows.

In the harness

A hosted harness with millions of users keeps transcripts, memories and vector indexes in N shards, chosen by a hash of tenant_id or by a directory for large customers. The session router derives the shard from the request's tenant, so a turn reads and writes one shard's transcript table and one tenant's vector namespace. This caps index size, contains a noisy enterprise tenant, and keeps one customer's memories physically separate from another's, which also helps meet data residency rules.

How it flows
  1. A turn request arrives carrying a tenant id.
  2. The router checks a pinned-tenant directory, otherwise hashes the id.
  3. The request is sent to that shard only.
  4. Transcript, memory and vector reads and writes all stay within it.
Sketch
SHARDS = [db_eu1, db_eu2, db_us1, db_us2]

def shard_for(tenant):
    if tenant in PINNED:     # big tenants
        return PINNED[tenant]
    h = int(sha1(tenant).hexdigest(), 16)
    return SHARDS[h % len(SHARDS)]

db = shard_for(req.tenant_id)
mems = db.memories.search(q, ns=req.user)

Watch outPlain modulo hashing moves almost every tenant when you add a shard; use consistent hashing or a directory, and keep queries that fan out to all shards off the hot path.

4.23

Client Session

Keep the conversation on the client, which sends the full message history with every request, so the server holds nothing between calls.

Analogy

The pilgrim's credential

Walkers on the Camino carry a small booklet that gets stamped at every hostel. The hostels keep no record of who passed through. Any hostel can see the whole journey so far by reading the booklet, and if the walker loses it, the record is gone.

Classic definition

Store session state on the client and send it to the server with every request, so the server keeps no per-session data.

In the harness

This is how a plain messages API works: the client keeps the messages array and sends all of it, with the system prompt and tool definitions, on every turn. Any server replica can serve any request, nothing needs expiring, and the client can edit, trim or branch its history freely. The costs are request size that grows every turn (prompt caching cuts the token price, not the bytes on the wire), trust, because a client can rewrite history including tool results, and loss if the client crashes before saving.

How it flows
  1. The client appends the user's message to its local history.
  2. It sends the entire history, system prompt and tools in one request.
  3. Whichever replica receives it calls the model and returns the reply.
  4. The client appends the reply; the server forgets the exchange.
Sketch
history = []        # lives in the client

def send(text):
    history.append({'role': 'user',
                    'content': text})
    r = client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL, system=SYSTEM,
        tools=TOOLS, messages=history)
    history.append({'role': 'assistant',
                    'content': r.content})
    return r

Watch outNever base security decisions on client-held history: a client can forge earlier tool_result blocks or approvals, so re-check permissions on the server.

4.24

Server Session

Keep the conversation, sandbox and files on the server under a session id; the client sends only the id and new message.

Analogy

The dry cleaner's ticket

You hand over a coat and get a small paper ticket with a number. The shop keeps the coat, its note about the wine stain and the promised date. You carry only the number, and any assistant at the counter can find your coat with it.

Classic definition

Keep session state on the server, identified by a session id that the client presents with each request.

In the harness

Hosted agent services keep the transcript, tool state, sandbox container and files on the server, keyed by session_id. The client sends {session_id, message} and streams back events. Requests stay small, the server is the authority on what really happened (tool results and approvals cannot be forged), and the same session can continue on another device. In exchange the server must store, expire, shard and guard sessions, and route each request to wherever that state lives.

How it flows
  1. The client posts a new message with its session id.
  2. The server checks that the caller owns the session and loads it.
  3. It runs the turn with the full server-held context and sandbox.
  4. It saves the session and streams the reply back to the client.
Sketch
@app.post('/sessions/{sid}/messages')
def post_message(sid, body, user):
    s = sessions.load(sid)
    if s.owner != user.id:
        raise Forbidden()
    s.messages.append(user_msg(body.text))
    reply = run_turn(s)     # server-side
    sessions.save(s)
    return stream(reply)

Watch outServer sessions need expiry, size limits and an owner check on every request; a guessable session id is a full transcript leak.

05
Chapter 5 · Many agents, one goal

Multi-Agent Orchestration

One agent hits limits of context and time. Many agents bring parallelism and specialisation, along with coordination, messaging and observability problems. These patterns come from distributed systems, where those problems were solved first.

Actor ModelMediatorMaster-WorkerFork/JoinFan-Out/Fan-InMapReduceLeader-FollowersLeader ElectionObserverPublish-SubscribeEvent AggregatorData BusPolling Pub/SubMicroservices MessagingMicroservices AggregatorSagaCommanderDistributed TracingLog AggregationSelf-RegistrationService Locator
5.01

Actor Model

Run each subagent as an isolated actor that owns its context and reacts only to messages in its mailbox.

Analogy

Lighthouse keepers and the mail boat

Each keeper lives alone on a rock with a private logbook nobody else reads. The only contact is the mail boat, which drops letters in a box on the jetty. The keeper opens them one at a time, acts, and sends replies back on the next boat. No keeper ever rows across to adjust another keeper's lamp.

Classic definition

Concurrent units called actors keep private state, communicate only by asynchronous messages, and process one message at a time from their mailbox.

In the harness

Each subagent runs with its own context window, system prompt and tool set, and the orchestrator cannot reach into that context directly. Work arrives as a message (a task brief) placed in the subagent's inbox, and the subagent's loop takes one message at a time, so its transcript never interleaves two tasks. Results travel the same way, as a message to the orchestrator's own inbox. Because nothing is shared, a crashed subagent can be restarted from its mailbox without corrupting anyone else's state.

How it flows
  1. The orchestrator sends a task message to the subagent's mailbox.
  2. The subagent dequeues one message and runs its loop inside its private context.
  3. It may send messages to other actors, including subagents it spawns.
  4. It posts a result message to the orchestrator's mailbox and takes the next message.
Sketch
class SubagentActor:
    def __init__(self, prompt):
        self.inbox = asyncio.Queue()
        self.ctx = [system(prompt)]  # private
    async def run(self):
        while True:
            m = await self.inbox.get()
            out = await turn(self.ctx, m.body)
            await m.reply_to.put(out)

coder.inbox.put_nowait(Msg(task, orc.inbox))

Watch outActors that wait synchronously on each other's replies can deadlock, so give every request a timeout and avoid request cycles between subagents.

5.02

Mediator

Route all subagent coordination through one orchestrator, so specialists never need to know about or message each other.

Analogy

The control tower

Pilots approaching a busy airport do not negotiate runway slots with each other over the radio. Each one talks only to the tower, which sees every aircraft and tells each pilot when to land, hold or taxi. A tenth plane arriving changes nobody else's instructions; the tower simply sequences one more.

Classic definition

Define an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact, so they refer to the mediator instead of to each other.

In the harness

In an orchestrator and subagent design, the researcher, coder, tester and reviewer subagents each report only to the orchestrator. The orchestrator holds the plan, decides who runs next, and turns one subagent's output into the next one's task brief, trimmed to what that subagent needs in its context. Direct chatter between subagents would multiply message paths, repeat context in every exchange and make the run hard to trace. Adding a specialist means teaching the orchestrator one more route, and the existing subagents stay unchanged.

How it flows
  1. A subagent finishes and returns its result to the orchestrator.
  2. The orchestrator records the result in the shared plan.
  3. It decides which specialist acts next and writes a focused brief for it.
  4. That subagent runs with only the brief and reports back the same way.
Sketch
class Orchestrator:
    def __init__(self, agents, plan):
        self.agents, self.plan = agents, plan
    def notify(self, sender, result):
        self.plan.record(sender, result)
        nxt = self.plan.next_step()
        if nxt:
            brief = self.brief_for(nxt, result)
            self.agents[nxt.role].send(brief)

Watch outA mediator that keeps every subagent's full output in its own context becomes a token bottleneck; store raw output in files and keep only summaries in the plan.

5.03

Master-Worker

A master agent splits a large job into independent tasks, hands them to worker subagents, and collects or reassigns the results.

Analogy

The orchard picking boss

At harvest the boss chalks a row number on each picker's bucket and keeps a clipboard of who has which row. Full crates come back to the boss's trailer. When a picker goes home sick at noon, the boss crosses out their name and gives the unfinished row to whoever is free next.

Classic definition

A master process divides work into tasks, distributes them to a pool of workers, gathers their results, and reassigns tasks whose workers fail.

In the harness

A migration agent that must update 300 files acts as master: it lists the files, groups them into batches and spawns a worker subagent per batch, each with a brief and a token budget. The master tracks every task's state (pending, running, done) in a task table. Workers return a short result message instead of their full transcripts, which keeps the master's context small. When a worker times out or its result fails a check, the master marks the batch pending again and gives it to the next free worker.

How it flows
  1. The master divides the job into independent tasks and records them as pending.
  2. It spawns workers up to a concurrency limit and assigns one task to each.
  3. Each worker runs in its own context and returns a compact result.
  4. The master marks tasks done, requeues failed or timed-out ones, and stops when the table is complete.
Sketch
tasks = {b.id: 'pending' for b in batches}
while 'pending' in tasks.values():
    for b in pending(tasks)[:MAX_WORKERS]:
        tasks[b.id] = 'running'
        spawn('migrator', b)
    for r in await finished(timeout=600):
        st = 'done' if r.ok else 'pending'
        tasks[r.id] = st

Watch outMaster-worker suits tasks that are truly independent; workers that edit the same files will overwrite each other's changes.

5.04

Fork/Join

Split a task into subtasks run by parallel subagents, possibly recursively, and continue only after every child has finished.

Analogy

The pit stop

The car stops and four crews leap at four wheels at once while another refuels. Nobody waves the car out when the first wheel is on. The crew chief lifts the board only when every crew has raised a hand, and then the car leaves as one.

Classic definition

Recursively divide a task into smaller subtasks that run in parallel (fork), then wait for all of them and combine their results (join).

In the harness

An agent asked to audit a monorepo forks one subagent per top-level package, and a subagent facing a large package may fork again per directory. Each parent then blocks on join: it waits for all of its children before summarising their findings and returning to its own parent. The harness enforces a maximum depth and a total subagent budget, because recursive forking multiplies token spend quickly. The join is a barrier, so the slowest child sets the pace for its parent.

How it flows
  1. The parent agent checks whether the task is small enough to do directly.
  2. If not, it splits the task and forks a child subagent for each part.
  3. Children run in parallel and may fork further within the depth limit.
  4. Each parent joins all its children, merges their results and returns upward.
Sketch
async def audit(path, depth=0):
    parts = split(path)
    if depth >= MAX_DEPTH or len(parts) < 2:
        return await run_agent('auditor', path)
    kids = [spawn(audit, p, depth + 1)
            for p in parts]  # fork
    res = await asyncio.gather(*kids)  # join
    return merge(res)

Watch outOne stuck child stalls its whole branch of the join, so give every forked subagent a timeout and decide in advance whether partial results are acceptable.

5.05

Fan-Out/Fan-In

Send the same question to several subagents at once, then gather their answers at one point, usually against a deadline.

Analogy

The exam bell

The invigilator hands the same paper to every student at the same moment. Each student works alone and in parallel. When the bell rings, the papers are collected into one pile whether or not the last student has finished, and only then does marking begin.

Classic definition

A dispatcher sends a request to many workers in parallel (fan-out) and a collector combines their responses into one result (fan-in).

In the harness

For a research question, the orchestrator fans out the same query to a web-search subagent, a code-search subagent and a docs subagent backed by an MCP server, all spawned in one turn. Fan-in happens at a collector that waits for every reply or for a deadline, whichever comes first. Late or failed replies are recorded as missing, so the orchestrator knows its answer rests on partial evidence. The collected replies then enter the orchestrator's context as one tool_result instead of three separate interruptions.

How it flows
  1. The orchestrator issues the same request to several subagents in parallel.
  2. Each subagent works independently with its own tools.
  3. A collector gathers replies until all arrive or the deadline passes.
  4. The orchestrator receives one combined bundle, with missing replies marked.
Sketch
jobs = [spawn(a, task=q) for a in
        ('web', 'code', 'docs')]
done, late = await asyncio.wait(
    jobs, timeout=60)
for j in late:
    j.cancel()
bundle = {'answers': [j.result() for j in done],
          'missing': len(late)}

Watch outFanning out multiplies the cost of every question, so fan out only when the sources are different enough to add new evidence.

5.06

MapReduce

Map each document through its own subagent to short notes, group the notes by theme, then reduce each group into one synthesis.

Analogy

Election night count

Every polling station counts its own ballot box and phones in one sheet of totals. At the regional centre the sheets are sorted by constituency and each pile is added up. The national result is built from those few sums, and nobody at the centre ever handles a paper ballot.

Classic definition

Process a large dataset by applying a map function to each record in parallel, grouping intermediate results by key, and combining each group with a reduce function.

In the harness

Forty PDFs will not fit in one context window, so the harness runs a map step: one subagent per document or chunk, all with the same summarisation prompt, each returning structured notes tagged with themes. The harness then groups the notes by theme, which is the shuffle step, and a reduce subagent per theme writes a synthesis from its notes alone. A final call merges the theme sections into the report. Every model call sees a bounded amount of text, so the job scales with the number of documents instead of the size of the context window.

How it flows
  1. Split the corpus into documents or chunks that each fit one context.
  2. Map: one subagent per chunk runs the same prompt and returns notes keyed by theme.
  3. Shuffle: the harness groups all notes by theme key.
  4. Reduce: one call per theme synthesises its notes, and a final call merges the sections.
Sketch
notes = await gather(*[
    run('summarise', d) for d in docs])
by_theme = defaultdict(list)
for n in chain(*notes):
    by_theme[n.theme].append(n)
parts = await gather(*[
    run('synthesise', t, ns)
    for t, ns in by_theme.items()])
report = await run('merge', parts)

Watch outMap summaries lose detail, so when the answer needs exact quotes or figures, carry source ids through the map step and let reducers look them up.

5.07

Leader-Followers

Worker agents take turns: one leader watches the task queue, claims the next task, then promotes a follower to lead.

Analogy

The taxi rank

Cabs queue nose to tail outside the station. Only the cab at the front picks up the next passenger. As it pulls away, the cab behind rolls forward and becomes the one to take the next fare. When the first driver drops off their passenger, they rejoin the back of the line.

Classic definition

A pool of threads shares a set of event sources; one leader waits for an event, promotes a follower to become the new leader, then processes the event itself.

In the harness

A fleet of identical worker agents serves a shared queue of tasks, such as incoming tickets or scheduled code reviews. Only the current leader polls the queue, so idle workers do not all hammer it and two workers never claim the same task. When the leader claims a task, it hands leadership to the next idle worker before starting its long model and tool calls, so the queue is never unwatched. When the worker finishes, it writes the result and rejoins the followers.

How it flows
  1. One idle worker holds the leader token and waits on the task queue.
  2. A task arrives and the leader claims it.
  3. The leader passes the token to the next follower, who starts waiting on the queue.
  4. The former leader processes the task, writes the result and rejoins the followers.
Sketch
async def worker(me, pool, queue):
    while True:
        await pool.wait_until_leader(me)
        task = await queue.claim()
        pool.promote_next()   # hand off lead
        out = await run_agent('review', task)
        results.write(task.id, out)
        pool.rejoin(me)

Watch outIf the leader crashes between claiming a task and promoting a follower, nobody watches the queue, so put a lease with a timeout on the leader token.

5.08

Leader Election

Let a fleet of identical agents agree on exactly one coordinator, and pick a new one automatically when it disappears.

Analogy

The conclave and the white smoke

The cardinals lock themselves in the chapel and vote until one name has the required majority. The ballots are burned after each round: black smoke means no decision, white smoke tells the crowd that there is one leader. When that leader dies, the same procedure runs again, and nobody acts as leader in between.

Classic definition

A distributed algorithm by which a group of nodes chooses a single node to coordinate them, and replaces it when it fails.

In the harness

When several harness instances share a task queue or run the same scheduled task, exactly one of them should coordinate: split the work, send reminders, write the daily summary. Each instance tries to acquire a lease in a shared store (a database row or key-value lock with a TTL), and the winner becomes leader and renews the lease while healthy. A term number rises with each new leader, and workers reject commands from an older term, which stops a paused former leader from acting on stale authority. If the leader's process crashes, its lease expires and another instance wins the next attempt.

How it flows
  1. Each agent instance tries to acquire the coordinator lease with a TTL.
  2. One succeeds, receives a new term number and starts coordinating.
  3. The leader renews the lease while healthy; the others keep retrying quietly.
  4. If renewals stop, the lease expires and the next instance to acquire it leads with a higher term.
Sketch
while running:
    got = store.acquire('coordinator',
                        me, ttl=30)
    if got:
        coordinate_round(term=got.term)
        store.renew('coordinator', me)
    await sleep(10)

Watch outNever elect by comparing clocks or by asking the model to pick a leader; use an atomic lease in a store that gives every instance the same answer.

5.09

Observer

Let the UI, the orchestrator and loggers watch a shared task list and react whenever a subagent changes an item.

Analogy

The coach's text list

The football coach keeps the parents' numbers in a list on her phone. When rain cancels Saturday's match, she updates the fixture and texts everyone on the list herself. Parents who join mid-season ask to be added, and nobody has to keep ringing the coach to ask whether the match is on.

Classic definition

A subject keeps a list of dependent observers and notifies each of them automatically when its state changes.

In the harness

The task list behind a todo tool is the subject. The chat UI's checklist panel, the orchestrator and the progress logger attach as observers when the run starts. When a subagent calls the tool to mark task 3 done, the task list updates itself and calls update on every attached observer: the panel redraws, the orchestrator considers what comes next, and the logger appends a line. Observers detach when the run ends, so finished sessions stop receiving updates.

How it flows
  1. The UI panel, orchestrator and logger call attach() on the task list.
  2. A subagent changes a task through a tool call.
  3. The task list stores the change and calls update() on each observer in its list.
  4. Each observer reads the new state and reacts in its own way.
Sketch
class TaskList:
    def __init__(self):
        self.items, self.observers = {}, []
    def attach(self, obs):
        self.observers.append(obs)
    def set_status(self, tid, status):
        self.items[tid] = status
        for o in self.observers:
            o.update(self, tid, status)

tasks.attach(checklist_panel)

Watch outObservers run inside the subject's call, so one slow observer (a remote logger, say) delays the subagent's tool result; hand slow work off asynchronously.

5.10

Publish-Subscribe

Agents publish events such as file.changed or task.done to named topics, and every agent subscribed to a topic receives them.

Analogy

Tuning in to a radio frequency

A station broadcasts traffic news on one frequency and music on another. It has no idea who is listening or how many. A taxi driver tunes to traffic, a hairdresser tunes to music, and a new listener can switch on at any moment without the station changing a thing.

Classic definition

Publishers send messages to topics without knowing the receivers, and a broker delivers each message to every subscriber of that topic.

In the harness

In a multi-agent coding run, the coder agent publishes file.changed with the path and a diff hash, and the test agent publishes task.done with its verdict. A broker inside the harness, or an external message service, keeps a subscriber list per topic. The lint agent and the index refresher both subscribe to file.changed, and the orchestrator subscribes to task.done. Publishers never address subscribers, so a new watcher such as a docs-updater agent joins by subscribing to an existing topic.

How it flows
  1. Subscribers register interest in topics with the broker.
  2. An agent publishes an event to a topic and carries on.
  3. The broker looks up the topic's subscribers.
  4. It delivers a copy to each one, and each handles it independently.
Sketch
bus.subscribe('file.changed', lint_agent)
bus.subscribe('file.changed', reindex)
bus.subscribe('task.done', orchestrator)

# inside the coder agent's write tool
bus.publish('file.changed',
            {'path': p, 'sha': sha})

Watch outEvents that wake agents can cause more events, so guard against loops such as a formatter agent whose own edits republish file.changed.

5.11

Event Aggregator

Collect events from every harness component in one hub, so listeners register once instead of wiring themselves to each source.

Analogy

The newsroom wire desk

Reports pour in from agencies, stringers and police scanners, and no editor watches every feed. Everything lands at the wire desk. The sports editor asks the desk for anything about football, the business editor asks for markets, and a new feed plugs into the desk without any editor noticing.

Classic definition

A single object receives events from many sources and lets subscribers register with it, instead of with each source individually.

In the harness

A harness has many event sources: the tool runner, the subagent pool, the file watcher, the permission gate and the model client's stream. Without a hub, the status bar, the transcript writer and the cost meter would each attach to every source. An event aggregator is the one object they all share: sources call hub.emit and listeners call hub.on with an event type. It usually lives in-process and runs handlers synchronously, unlike a networked pub-sub broker, and it gives one place to add filtering, ordering or recording.

How it flows
  1. At startup, listeners register handlers with the hub by event type.
  2. Components emit events to the hub as things happen.
  3. The hub looks up the handlers for that event type.
  4. It calls each handler in registration order.
Sketch
class EventHub:
    def __init__(self):
        self.handlers = defaultdict(list)
    def on(self, kind, fn):
        self.handlers[kind].append(fn)
    def emit(self, kind, **data):
        for fn in self.handlers[kind]:
            fn(**data)

hub.on('tool.done', cost_meter.add)
tool_runner.hub = subagents.hub = hub

Watch outWhen everything talks only to the hub, it gets hard to see who reacts to what, so keep a generated list of event types and their handlers.

5.12

Data Bus

Connect every agent to one shared bus that carries all messages, and let each member decide which messages it acts on.

Analogy

The site radio channel

On a building site everyone carries a walkie-talkie tuned to one channel. When the crane driver says a load is swinging over the east side, the scaffolders hear it, the electricians hear it, and so does the tea van. Each person decides whether the message concerns them, and nobody keeps a list of who should be told.

Classic definition

Components attach to a common bus and communicate by posting messages onto it; every attached member sees every message and filters for itself.

In the harness

A small agent team can share one in-process bus: the planner, coder, tester, a UI panel and the transcript writer all attach to it. Every message (plan.updated, file.saved, tests.failed) goes onto the bus and reaches all members, and each checks the type and ignores what it does not handle. There is no routing table, which keeps things simple while the team and the message volume are small. The bus is also a single point at which to record every message into the transcript for replay.

How it flows
  1. Each agent attaches to the bus when it starts.
  2. An agent posts a typed message onto the bus.
  3. The bus hands the message to every attached member.
  4. Each member filters by message type and acts only on those it handles.
Sketch
class DataBus:
    def __init__(self):
        self.members = []
    def attach(self, m):
        self.members.append(m)
    def post(self, msg):
        for m in self.members:
            m.receive(msg)

class Tester(Member):
    def receive(self, msg):
        if msg.type == 'file.saved':
            self.queue_tests(msg.path)

Watch outEvery member receives every message, so the bus scales badly; once members ignore most of the traffic, move to topics or an event aggregator.

5.13

Polling Pub/Sub

Publishers append events to a shared store, and each subscriber agent polls it on its own schedule using a saved cursor.

Analogy

The post office box

Letters for you go into a numbered box at the post office, and the postman never knocks on your door. You call in when it suits you, on the way to work or once a week, and take everything that arrived since your last visit. If you are away for a fortnight, the letters simply wait.

Classic definition

Publishers write messages to a durable topic, and subscribers periodically pull the messages that arrived after their last read position.

In the harness

Agents that run as scheduled tasks or short sessions cannot hold a push connection open, so the harness writes events to an append-only table or file with increasing ids. Each subscriber keeps a cursor, the id of the last event it handled, and on each wake-up asks for events after that cursor. A subagent that was asleep, crashed, or paused waiting for user approval catches up on its next poll. The cost is latency up to the polling interval, plus wasted calls when nothing has changed.

How it flows
  1. A publisher appends an event with the next sequence id.
  2. A subscriber wakes on its interval and requests events after its cursor.
  3. It handles the returned events in order.
  4. It saves the new cursor, so a restart resumes from the right place.
Sketch
cursor = state.get('cursor', 0)
while True:
    events = store.read(topic='repo',
                        after=cursor)
    for ev in events:
        handle(ev)
        cursor = ev.id
    state.save('cursor', cursor)
    await sleep(POLL_SECONDS)

Watch outSave the cursor only after handling succeeds, or a crash between reading and handling will silently skip events.

5.14

Microservices Messaging

Agent services talk through asynchronous message channels, so a sender posts work and moves on without waiting for the receiver.

Analogy

The department store's pneumatic tubes

A shop assistant rolls the cash and the receipt into a canister, drops it into a tube and turns to the next customer. The canister shoots off to the counting house, which deals with it when it can. If the counting house is busy, canisters pile up in its basket, none are lost, and the shop floor never waits.

Classic definition

Services communicate by sending messages over asynchronous channels such as queues or streams, which decouples them in time and availability.

In the harness

A research service and a writing service, each its own agent deployment, are connected by a durable queue called research.results. The research agent sends a message with its findings and a correlation id, then picks up its next job without waiting. The writer consumes messages at its own pace and acknowledges each one only after it has saved its draft, and unacknowledged messages are redelivered. A message that fails repeatedly moves to a dead-letter queue for a person or a repair agent to inspect.

How it flows
  1. The producer agent sends a message with a correlation id to the channel.
  2. The channel stores it durably and the producer moves on.
  3. The consumer receives the message, does the work and acknowledges it.
  4. Unacknowledged messages are redelivered, and repeated failures go to a dead-letter queue.
Sketch
# research service
chan.send('research.results',
    {'cid': job.id, 'findings': notes})

# writer service
for msg in chan.consume('research.results'):
    try:
        draft = write(msg.body['findings'])
        drafts.save(msg.body['cid'], draft)
        msg.ack()
    except Exception:
        msg.nack()   # redeliver, then DLQ

Watch outChannels deliver at least once, so consumers must tolerate duplicates, for example by keying saved drafts on the correlation id.

5.15

Microservices Aggregator

One aggregator calls several specialist subagents, then merges their partial outputs into a single answer for the user.

Analogy

The travel agent's holiday folder

You ask for a week in Crete. The agent rings the airline for flights, the hotel for a room and the hire firm for a car, then hands you one folder with a single itinerary and a single price. You never hear the three phone calls, and if no car was available, the folder says so on one line.

Classic definition

A service receives a request, calls several backend services, and combines their responses into one reply for the client.

In the harness

When a user asks for a release readiness report, the aggregator agent sends focused requests to a test-results subagent, a changelog subagent and a security-scan subagent. Each returns structured output against a schema the aggregator defined. The aggregator reconciles them, removes duplicates, flags conflicts (two subagents disagreeing about a version number) and writes one reply or artifact. The user and the chat UI talk to one endpoint and never need to know how many subagents produced the answer.

How it flows
  1. The user's request reaches the aggregator.
  2. It sends a focused sub-request to each specialist subagent.
  3. Each subagent returns structured partial output.
  4. The aggregator merges and reconciles the parts and returns one answer, naming any missing part.
Sketch
async def readiness(release):
    tests, log, scan = await gather(
        ask('tests', release),
        ask('changelog', release),
        ask('security', release),
        return_exceptions=True)
    parts = {'tests': tests, 'log': log,
             'scan': scan}
    return render_report(merge(parts))

Watch outThe aggregator is the only place where a partial failure is visible, so it must say which section is missing instead of smoothing over the gap.

5.16

Saga

Run a multi-step workflow across agents as a chain of local steps, each paired with a compensating action that undoes it.

Analogy

Booking a wedding

The couple books the venue, then the caterer, paying a deposit each time, and then tries to book a band. No band is free that weekend, and there is no single undo button. So they ring the caterer to cancel, then the venue, each under its own cancellation terms, working back through the bookings in reverse order.

Classic definition

Manage a long-running transaction across services as a sequence of local transactions, where a failure triggers compensating transactions for the steps already completed.

In the harness

A release workflow spans a coder agent that creates a branch, a database agent that runs a migration on staging, and a deploy agent that ships to staging. No transaction covers git, a database and a deploy tool at once, so each step commits on its own and registers a compensation: delete the branch, run the down-migration. A saga log records which steps finished. When the deploy fails, the coordinator reads the log, runs the compensations in reverse order and reports the state the system was left in.

How it flows
  1. The coordinator runs step 1 and records it, with its compensation, in the saga log.
  2. It continues step by step, recording each success.
  3. A step fails and the coordinator stops moving forward.
  4. It runs the compensations of the completed steps in reverse order and logs the outcome.
Sketch
steps = [(create_branch, delete_branch),
         (migrate_db, migrate_down),
         (deploy, None)]
done = []
for action, undo in steps:
    try:
        action(ctx); done.append(undo)
        log.write(action.__name__, 'ok')
    except StepFailed:
        for u in reversed(done):
            if u: u(ctx)
        raise

Watch outA compensation is a new forward action and cannot unsend an email, so plan a correction step for any effect that is impossible to reverse.

5.17

Commander

A commander agent drives a distributed transaction to completion, retrying failed steps from a durable log until every service succeeds.

Analogy

The stage manager's cue calls

During the show the stage manager calls each cue over the headset, 'lights twelve, go', and waits to hear 'lights done'. If the sound desk does not answer, she calls again, and keeps calling until it does. Every confirmed cue is ticked in the prompt book, so if she is replaced at the interval, her deputy knows exactly where the show is.

Classic definition

A coordinator manages a transaction across several services by tracking each step's state, retrying failures with backoff, and recording progress so it can resume after a crash.

In the harness

Publishing a release means pushing a tag to the repository service, uploading a package to a registry and posting release notes through a messaging connector. Unlike a saga, the commander aims to finish: when the registry returns a 503, it schedules that step for retry with backoff and keeps the tag. It writes each step's state to a durable transaction log, so a harness restart picks up the half-finished transaction. A step that exhausts its retries escalates to a person through the approval UI.

How it flows
  1. The commander records a new transaction and its steps as pending.
  2. It calls each service in turn and records every success.
  3. A failed step is retried later with backoff.
  4. Retries continue until every step succeeds, or a step escalates to a person after its retry limit.
Sketch
txn = log.begin(['push_tag', 'publish',
                 'post_notes'])
for step in txn.pending():
    for attempt in range(MAX_TRIES):
        if call(step, txn.data).ok:
            log.mark(txn, step, 'done')
            break
        await sleep(backoff(attempt))
    else:
        escalate(txn, step)

Watch outRetrying until success is safe only for idempotent steps, so give every call an idempotency key or a retry may publish the package twice.

5.18

Distributed Tracing

Carry one trace id through the orchestrator, subagents, tool calls and model calls, so a whole run reads as one tree.

Analogy

The parcel tracking number

Your parcel gets one number at the counter. Every depot, van and sorting belt that touches it scans the number and adds a line with a time and a place. When the parcel is late, you type the number in once and see the whole journey, including the six hours it sat in a depot nobody suspected.

Classic definition

Propagate a trace context with every request across services, so each unit of work records a span with its parent, and the spans assemble into one end-to-end trace.

In the harness

When a user message starts a run, the harness creates a trace id and a root span for the orchestrator's turn. Spawning a subagent passes the trace id and parent span id in the task envelope, and every model call and tool call inside the subagent opens a child span with timing, token counts and status. MCP requests carry the same context in their metadata, so remote servers can attach their spans too. A collector assembles the spans into a tree that shows which subagent spent the tokens or which tool call stalled the run.

How it flows
  1. The harness creates a trace id and a root span when the run starts.
  2. Every spawn, model call and tool call opens a child span carrying the trace id and its parent's span id.
  3. Each span records timing, tokens and status when it closes.
  4. A collector assembles all spans with the same trace id into one tree.
Sketch
with tracer.span('orchestrator') as root:
    ctx = root.context  # trace_id, span_id
    sub = spawn('researcher', task,
                trace=ctx)

# inside the subagent's harness
with tracer.span('model.call', parent=ctx):
    r = client.messages.create(**req)
with tracer.span('tool.web_search',
                 parent=ctx):
    run_tool(block)

Watch outSpans that store full prompts and tool outputs copy secrets into the observability store, so record sizes and hashes by default and full content only on opt-in.

5.19

Log Aggregation

Ship logs from every agent run, subagent and MCP server to one central store, indexed by run id, for search and alerts.

Analogy

The hospital records office

Every department writes its own notes on the patient: the emergency room, the X-ray suite, the surgical ward. When the patient goes home, all those sheets go to the records office and are filed under one hospital number. Months later a doctor asks for that number and reads the whole stay in date order.

Classic definition

Services send their logs to a central logging service that stores and indexes them, so operators can search across all of them in one place.

In the harness

A busy harness runs hundreds of agent sessions across many workers, and each session's subagents, sandboxes and MCP servers write their own logs. A shipper on each host forwards structured JSON lines to a central log store, adding the run id, agent name, host and timestamp. Operators search one place for every error from a given tool, and evals or alert rules query the same data, for example a rising rate of permission denials. Without aggregation, debugging a failed run starts with working out which machine each subagent happened to run on.

How it flows
  1. Every component writes structured log lines tagged with the run id.
  2. A shipper on each host forwards the lines to the central store.
  3. The store indexes them by run id, component, level and time.
  4. People and alert rules query across all runs from one place.
Sketch
log = logger.bind(run_id=run.id,
                  agent='researcher')
log.info('tool.start', tool='web_search')
log.warn('permission.denied', path=p)

# central query across all runs
store.query('level:warn AND'
            ' event:permission.denied'
            ' | count by agent')

Watch outAgent logs grow quickly and often hold user data, so set retention limits and redact secrets before the lines leave the host.

5.20

Self-Registration

Each agent service or MCP server announces its name, address and tools to a registry at startup, and keeps renewing that entry.

Analogy

Signing in with the market warden

Stallholders at a street market arrive at dawn and sign the warden's book: pitch number, name, and what they sell. Shoppers ask the warden where to find cheese. Traders wave at the warden's hut every few hours, and anyone not seen by noon is crossed off, so shoppers are never sent to an empty pitch.

Classic definition

A service instance registers itself with the service registry on startup, renews its registration with heartbeats, and deregisters on shutdown.

In the harness

When an MCP server or a specialist agent service boots, it calls the harness registry with its name, endpoint and tool list (search_issues, create_issue) plus a TTL. It sends a heartbeat before the TTL runs out and deregisters on a clean shutdown. Orchestrators query the registry to decide which tools or agents to offer the model on the next turn. Entries whose heartbeats stop are evicted, so a crashed server drops out of the tool list instead of producing failed tool calls.

How it flows
  1. The service starts and registers its name, endpoint and tool list with a TTL.
  2. It sends heartbeats to renew the entry.
  3. Orchestrators query the registry to discover live capabilities.
  4. If heartbeats stop, the registry evicts the entry.
Sketch
async def main():
    server = McpServer('issues', tools)
    await registry.register(
        name='issues', url=server.url,
        tools=[t.name for t in tools], ttl=30)
    async with every(10, registry.renew,
                     'issues'):
        await server.serve()
    await registry.deregister('issues')

Watch outA registry entry is only a claim, so check that the server's live tool schemas match what it registered before exposing them to the model.

5.21

Service Locator

Code asks a central locator for a connector or agent by name at runtime, instead of wiring each dependency in.

Analogy

Ringing directory enquiries

You need a plumber in a town you have never visited. You ring directory enquiries, give a name, and the operator reads you a number. You do not need every phone book in the country, and if the plumber moves, the operator gives you the new number next time.

Classic definition

A central registry object that code calls to obtain a service by name, hiding how the service is created or found.

In the harness

Skills and subagent code often need a connector they did not create: the web search MCP client, the issue tracker, a reviewer subagent. They call locator.get('issues'), and the locator returns a live client from its cache or builds one from the factory registered under that name. A skill written once can then run in harnesses with different connectors installed, as long as the names match. The cost is hidden dependencies: you cannot tell which connectors a piece of code needs until it runs.

How it flows
  1. At startup the harness registers a factory for each name in the locator.
  2. Code calls get(name) when it needs a connector or agent.
  3. The locator returns a cached client or builds one from the factory.
  4. An unknown name raises a clear error that the harness reports back to the model.
Sketch
class Locator:
    def __init__(self, table):
        self.table, self.live = table, {}
    def get(self, name):
        if name not in self.live:
            make = self.table[name]
            self.live[name] = make()
        return self.live[name]

issues = locator.get('issues')

Watch outA locator hides what code depends on, so prefer explicit injection in the harness core and keep the locator for plugins and skills loaded at runtime.

06
Chapter 6 · Work that waits

Async, Concurrency and Scheduling

Agents wait on models, tools, people and clocks. These patterns let a harness keep many runs in flight, hand work to background workers, pause for approval and shut down cleanly without races.

PromiseAsync Method InvocationEvent-Based AsynchronousProducer-ConsumerEvent QueueActive ObjectReactorThread-Pool ExecutorThread-Specific StorageGuarded SuspensionBalkingPoison PillHalf-Sync/Half-AsyncMonitorLockable ObjectDouble-Checked LockingDouble Buffer
6.01

Promise

Hand back a placeholder for a result that will arrive later, so the caller keeps working instead of blocking.

Analogy

The buzzer at a food court

You order, pay, and get a plastic buzzer. You do not stand at the counter; you find a seat and talk. When the food is ready the buzzer goes off and you collect it. If the kitchen runs out, the buzzer flashes a different light and you go back to sort it out.

Classic definition

An object representing the eventual result of an asynchronous operation, which callers can chain or await.

In the harness

When the main agent launches a background subagent, the harness immediately returns a handle (an agent id) instead of the finished report. The orchestrator keeps planning or answering the user, and when the subagent completes, the harness resolves the handle and injects a notification into the conversation. A failed subagent rejects the handle with an error the orchestrator can handle.

How it flows
  1. The orchestrator calls spawn_agent and immediately gets a pending handle.
  2. It continues other work while the subagent runs.
  3. The subagent finishes and the harness resolves the handle.
  4. A completion notice arrives and the orchestrator reads the result.
Sketch
# returns at once with a pending handle
h = harness.spawn('researcher', task=q)
plan_next_steps()

# resolves when the subagent finishes
report = await h
h.on_error(lambda e: log.warn(e))

Watch outNever invent or guess the value of an unresolved promise; if the user asks early, say the work is still running.

6.02

Async Method Invocation

Start a slow job such as a background subagent, get a future back at once, and collect the result when it is needed.

Analogy

Dropping film at the photo lab

You hand your roll of film over the counter and get a numbered claim stub. You do not stand there while the prints develop; you go and do your shopping. Later you either come back with the stub and ask if they are ready, or the lab rings the number on the stub. The stub is the only link between you and the job.

Classic definition

Invoke a method on another thread so the caller immediately receives a future or callback hook while the work runs.

In the harness

When the model calls a tool such as run_in_background or launches a background subagent, the harness submits the job to an executor and puts a task id in the tool_result straight away. The model carries on with other tool calls in the same turn. Later it can poll a status tool with the id, await the future, or rely on a completion callback that injects the result into the transcript as a new message. Because the invoker owns the thread or task, it can also cancel the job or enforce a timeout.

How it flows
  1. The model calls run_in_background with a task description.
  2. The invoker submits the job to an executor and returns a task id at once.
  3. The model makes other tool calls while the job runs.
  4. It polls the status tool, or a done-callback injects the result into the transcript.
Sketch
fut = executor.submit(run_subagent, task)
return {'task_id': fut.id}

# a later turn: poll, or let a callback fire
if fut.done():
    report = fut.result()
else:
    fut.add_done_callback(inject_result)

Watch outA background job that nobody awaits or cancels leaks; track every future per session and cancel or report the stragglers when the session ends.

6.03

Event-Based Asynchronous

Expose a long job as start, progress, completed, failed and cancel events, so the UI and agent loop react as things happen.

Analogy

The pharmacy text alerts

You drop off a prescription and leave your phone number. A text arrives when it is being made up, another if an item is out of stock, and a last one when it is ready to collect. If you no longer need it you reply STOP. You never stand at the counter asking whether it is done yet.

Classic definition

Provide a MethodAsync call that returns at once and raises ProgressChanged and Completed events on the caller's context, with optional cancellation.

In the harness

A background subagent, a long build or a scheduled task publishes lifecycle events: started, progress, completed, failed, cancelled. The chat UI subscribes to progress to update a task card, and the agent loop subscribes to completed and failed so it can add a task-notification message to the conversation. Cancellation flows the other way as a cancel request on the same task id. The runner raises events back on the session's own event loop, so handlers never touch session state from a worker thread.

How it flows
  1. The caller starts the job with run_async and gets a task id.
  2. The worker raises progress events as it goes.
  3. On finish it raises completed with the result, or failed with the error.
  4. Handlers on the session loop update the task card and notify the model.
Sketch
task = runner.run_async(job, task_id='t42')
task.on('progress', ui.update_card)
task.on('completed', lambda r:
        transcript.notify(f'done: {r}'))
task.on('failed', lambda e:
        transcript.notify(f'failed: {e}'))

# user presses Stop on the task card
task.cancel_async()

Watch outEvents fire once, so a handler registered after completed has fired misses the result; subscribe before starting, or let late subscribers read the last state.

6.04

Producer-Consumer

Let many sources put agent jobs into a bounded buffer while a separate set of workers takes them off at its own pace.

Analogy

The bakery cooling rack

Bakers slide fresh trays onto a tall cooling rack; shop staff lift trays off the other side to stock the counter. Nobody hands bread from person to person. When every shelf is full the bakers wait, and when the rack is empty the staff wait. The number of shelves decides how far ahead the ovens can run.

Classic definition

Decouple producers from consumers through a shared bounded buffer that blocks producers when full and consumers when empty.

In the harness

Webhook handlers, cron-fired scheduled tasks and user messages from many sessions all produce agent jobs. Instead of calling the agent loop directly, they put jobs on a bounded asyncio.Queue or a broker list. A fixed set of consumer workers take jobs, run the model and tool calls, and store the results. When the queue is full, producers wait or answer 429, which shields model rate limits and token budgets from bursts.

How it flows
  1. Producers wrap incoming work as job messages.
  2. They put jobs on a bounded queue, waiting if it is full.
  3. Consumers take one job at a time, waiting if it is empty.
  4. Each consumer runs the agent turn and records the result.
Sketch
jobs = asyncio.Queue(maxsize=100)

async def on_webhook(evt):     # producer
    await jobs.put(Job.from_event(evt))

async def worker():            # consumer
    while True:
        job = await jobs.get()
        await run_agent(job)
        jobs.task_done()

Watch outAn unbounded queue hides overload until memory runs out; always set a size and decide whether producers wait, drop or reject.

6.05

Event Queue

Buffer events that arrive mid-turn so the agent loop handles them in order at a safe point, instead of the moment they happen.

Analogy

The radio request line

Listeners phone in song requests while a track is playing. The producer writes each one on a card and adds it to the back of a pile in the booth. The DJ never cuts a song off halfway; between tracks they take the next card from the front of the pile and play it.

Classic definition

Decouple when an event is sent from when it is processed by placing it in a queue the receiver drains in its own time.

In the harness

While the model is streaming or a tool is running, other things keep happening: the user types a follow-up, a background subagent finishes, a file watcher fires, a scheduled trigger arrives. Handling each one immediately would splice it into the middle of the current turn and corrupt the transcript. So the harness appends each to a per-session event queue and returns. At the turn boundary the agent loop drains the queue in arrival order and converts the events into messages before the next model call.

How it flows
  1. A sender posts an event to the session queue and returns immediately.
  2. The current model call or tool call continues undisturbed.
  3. At the turn boundary the loop drains queued events in arrival order.
  4. Each event becomes a message in the context for the next model call.
Sketch
inbox = collections.deque()

def post(event):        # any hook or thread
    inbox.append(event)

def at_turn_boundary(ctx):
    while inbox:
        ev = inbox.popleft()
        ctx.messages.append(ev.to_message())

Watch outIf events arrive faster than turns finish, coalesce or cap them, or the next prompt fills with stale notices.

6.06

Active Object

Give a scheduled task its own thread and request queue, so callers enqueue method requests and get futures back.

Analogy

The assistant's in-tray

You do not interrupt the executive assistant mid-task. You drop a note in their in-tray and keep a carbon copy as your receipt. They take notes from the tray one at a time and put each answer in the sender's pigeonhole. Their work always happens at their own desk, never at yours.

Classic definition

Decouple invocation from execution: a proxy turns calls into requests on an activation queue, and a scheduler runs them on the object's own thread, resolving futures.

In the harness

A scheduled task such as a daily inbox triage runs as an active object: it owns a session, a transcript and a single worker thread or asyncio task. Callers, whether the cron trigger, a Run now button or another agent, never touch that session directly. They call a proxy method run(prompt), which wraps the call as a request, puts it on the task's activation queue and returns a future. The task's scheduler takes requests in order, runs each turn against its own session, and resolves the matching future.

How it flows
  1. A caller invokes proxy.run(prompt) and receives a future.
  2. The proxy puts a method request on the activation queue.
  3. The scheduler on the task's thread takes the next request.
  4. The servant runs the turn in its own session and resolves the future.
Sketch
class ScheduledTask:          # proxy side
    def run(self, prompt):
        fut = Future()
        self.q.put((prompt, fut))
        return fut

    def _loop(self):          # own thread
        while True:
            prompt, fut = self.q.get()
            out = self.session.turn(prompt)
            fut.set_result(out)

Watch outIf code running on the task's own thread calls its proxy and waits on the future, it deadlocks, because the request queues behind itself.

6.07

Reactor

Run one event loop that waits on many streaming connections at once and dispatches each ready event to its handler.

Analogy

The switchboard operator

One operator sits in front of a panel of sockets. They do not watch any single line; they wait for a lamp to light. When one does, they plug in the cord for that caller, deal with it in seconds, and turn back to the panel. Hundreds of lines share one pair of hands because each job is short.

Classic definition

Demultiplex events from many handles with a single synchronous wait, then dispatch each one to a registered, non-blocking handler.

In the harness

A harness server holds thousands of open connections: SSE streams from the model provider, WebSocket links to chat clients, stdio pipes to local MCP servers. A single asyncio event loop registers them all with the OS selector (epoll or kqueue). When a socket has bytes, the loop calls that connection's handler, which appends a token delta, forwards it to the right client, or parses a JSON-RPC reply. Handlers must return quickly, so CPU-heavy work such as tokenising a large file is pushed to a thread pool.

How it flows
  1. Each connection registers a handler with the event loop.
  2. The loop blocks once in select or epoll across all handles.
  3. For each ready handle it calls the registered handler.
  4. Handlers do a small non-blocking step and return to the loop.
Sketch
sel = selectors.DefaultSelector()
sel.register(model_sse, READ, on_token)
sel.register(client_ws, READ, on_user_msg)
sel.register(mcp_pipe, READ, on_rpc_reply)

while running:
    for key, _ in sel.select():
        key.data(key.fileobj)   # dispatch

Watch outOne blocking call inside a handler, such as a synchronous HTTP request, freezes every stream on the loop.

6.08

Thread-Pool Executor

Run tool calls or whole sessions on a fixed set of reusable workers, so extra load queues up instead of spawning unbounded threads.

Analogy

The taxi rank

A rank has a fixed number of licensed cabs. Passengers join one queue at the stand, and each cab that pulls in takes whoever is at the front. On a busy night the queue grows, but the town never gets a hundred extra taxis clogging the streets, and no cab is built for one ride and scrapped.

Classic definition

Keep a pool of worker threads that take tasks from a shared queue, reusing threads and capping concurrency.

In the harness

When the model returns several tool_use blocks in one turn, the harness submits them to a ThreadPoolExecutor with, say, max_workers=8, then gathers the results and orders them by call id for the tool_result message. A server hosting many sessions applies the same idea at a larger grain: N worker processes, each running one agent session at a time. Pool size becomes the single knob for CPU, sandbox count and concurrent model requests.

How it flows
  1. The harness creates a pool with a fixed number of workers.
  2. Each tool_use block is submitted as a task to the pool's queue.
  3. Free workers take tasks; the rest wait in the queue.
  4. The harness collects results by call id and builds the tool_result message.
Sketch
pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8)

futs = {pool.submit(run_tool, b): b.id
        for b in blocks}
results = {}
for f in as_completed(futs):
    results[futs[f]] = f.result()
reply = [results[b.id] for b in blocks]

Watch outTasks that wait on each other inside one small pool can deadlock it; keep dependent steps out of the pool or size it with care.

6.09

Thread-Specific Storage

Give each session its own slot for user id, budget and trace id, readable from shared worker code without passing it everywhere.

Analogy

Each cashier's own till drawer

Six cashiers share one shop, one price list and one row of tills. Each logs in with their own key, and the drawer that springs open is always theirs, with their float and their takings. The screen in front of them is identical; the money is never mixed.

Classic definition

Let code access a logically global variable whose value is private to the current thread or task.

In the harness

A harness server runs many sessions on one asyncio loop and a shared thread pool. Deep inside, a tool wrapper needs to know which session it serves: the user id for permission checks, the token budget, the trace id, the sandbox path. Rather than threading those through every function signature, the harness sets a contextvars.ContextVar at the start of each session task. Any code running in that task, including logging and the MCP client, calls session.get() and sees its own values, even while another session's task interleaves on the same thread.

How it flows
  1. The server declares a ContextVar for session state.
  2. Each session task sets it at start with its own values.
  3. Shared tool and logging code calls get() to read the current session.
  4. The value disappears with the task, so nothing leaks to the next session.
Sketch
session = ContextVar('session')

async def handle(req):
    session.set(Session(req.user, budget=5e4))
    await agent_loop(req)

def write_file(path, text):   # shared code
    s = session.get()
    s.sandbox.check(path)

Watch outContext does not follow into raw threads you start yourself; use copy_context() or run_in_executor, or the worker sees the wrong session or none.

6.10

Guarded Suspension

Suspend an action until its precondition holds, such as waiting for the user's approval before running a risky tool.

Analogy

A train held at a red signal

A driver reaches a red signal and stops. They do not creep forward or guess; they wait. When the signaller clears the section ahead, the light turns green and the train moves off. If the light flickers, the driver checks it again before releasing the brake.

Classic definition

Block a method call until a guard condition becomes true, waiting on a condition variable and re-checking after each wake-up.

In the harness

When the model calls a tool marked as needing permission, such as sending an email or deleting files, the harness records a pending approval and suspends that tool call on a condition. The chat UI shows an approval card. When the user clicks Allow or Deny, the UI handler sets the decision and notifies the waiting coroutine, which re-checks the guard and either runs the tool or returns a denial as the tool_result. A timeout turns a long silence into a denial rather than an indefinite hang.

How it flows
  1. The tool call reaches the gate while its decision is still unset.
  2. The harness posts an approval card and waits on a condition.
  3. The user's click sets the decision and notifies the waiter.
  4. The call wakes, re-checks the guard, and runs or returns a denial.
Sketch
async def guarded_run(call):
    async with cond:
        await cond.wait_for(
            lambda: call.decision is not None)
    if call.decision != 'allow':
        return denied(call)
    return await call.tool.run(call.args)

async def on_click(call, choice):   # UI
    async with cond:
        call.decision = choice
        cond.notify_all()

Watch outAlways pair the wait with a timeout that denies by default, or a forgotten approval card holds a worker and a sandbox forever.

6.11

Balking

If the object is not in the right state, return at once instead of waiting: skip a run when one is already in flight.

Analogy

The lit lift button

You reach the lift and the call button is already glowing because someone pressed it a moment ago. Pressing it again changes nothing; the lift is already on its way. The button does not summon a second lift or make you wait at the panel. It simply ignores the extra press.

Classic definition

Perform an action only if the object is in a suitable state, and otherwise return immediately without doing anything.

In the harness

A scheduled task fires every 15 minutes, but one run sometimes takes 20. Without care the scheduler starts an overlapping run on the same session, doubling model spend and racing on the transcript. With balking, the trigger handler checks a running flag under a lock: if a run is in flight it logs 'skipped: already running' and returns. The same check stops a double-click on Send from launching two turns, and stops a second compaction while one is underway.

How it flows
  1. The trigger fires and calls start_run.
  2. Under a lock, the handler checks whether a run is already active.
  3. If one is, it logs a skip and returns immediately.
  4. Otherwise it marks the run active, starts it, and clears the flag when done.
Sketch
def start_run(task):
    with task.lock:
        if task.running:
            log.info('balk: run in flight')
            return 'skipped'
        task.running = True
    try:
        execute(task)
    finally:
        task.running = False

Watch outBalking silently drops requests, so use it only when the skipped request is truly redundant; if every request matters, queue it instead.

6.12

Poison Pill

Shut down queue workers cleanly by sending a special stop message that each worker recognises and exits on.

Analogy

The marathon sweep bus

Behind the last runner of a marathon drives the sweep bus. Volunteers at each water station keep handing out cups until it passes; when they see it, they know nobody else is coming and pack up the tables. Nobody phones the stations. The signal travels along the course in the same stream as the runners.

Classic definition

Place a sentinel message in a queue so each consumer knows to finish its current work and stop when it reaches it.

In the harness

When a harness host deploys a new version or a batch eval finishes, it must stop its agent workers without abandoning half-run turns. The supervisor stops accepting new jobs, then puts one STOP sentinel per worker on the job queue. Each worker finishes the job it holds and the jobs ahead of the pill in FIFO order, then exits its loop when it takes STOP. The supervisor joins the workers, flushes transcripts and closes MCP connections.

How it flows
  1. The supervisor stops accepting new jobs.
  2. It enqueues one STOP sentinel per worker behind the remaining jobs.
  3. Workers process the jobs ahead of the pill as usual.
